The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most everyday devices. Interacting with external peripherals is an essential aspect of embedded software, which often relies on dynamic, unpredictable inputs. When testing this software, the behavior of external components can introduce randomness and make a system difficult to model. This is particularly true during development when the software is still evolving and being refined. To address these challenges, a new method is proposed, utilizing Model-Based Testing to improve the coverage and effectiveness of software quality assurance. This method leverages a modular structure, separating the model into internal and external components, which enables the use of traditional Model Checking and testing tools. By doing so, the complexity of modeling external interactions is avoided, allowing developers to focus on the software itself. The proposed approach is demonstrated through a practical example, showcasing its application to a real-world embedded system. The results of this experiment indicate that the test suite created using Model-Based Testing meets high standards, covering a substantial portion of the software's features. Furthermore, when simulated faults are introduced, the test suite successfully detects and identifies nearly all introduced errors. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method in a real-world setting, an empirical study was conducted. The findings of this study, involving 12 participants and 18 programs, reveal a positive correlation between the complexity of model-based test coverage and the effectiveness of the test suite. Notably, when test coverage increases, so does the proportion of detected faults. While there is a marginal improvement in programs with moderate complexity, those with high complexity see a substantial and consistent enhancement in detection rates. To facilitate future studies and evaluations, the associated data and test results have been made publicly available. Based on these findings, model-based testing can be an effective quality assurance strategy, particularly for embedded software with complex external interactions. When implemented, it can yield impressive results, as demonstrated by the significant improvement in detection rates and simplicity of test coverage. Ultimately, the proposed approach offers a valuable contribution to the field, offering a practical and achievable method for ensuring the quality of embedded software through model-based testing. To facilitate adoption, a supporting tool has been developed and made available for download. When implemented, it can yield impressive results, as demonstrated by the significant improvement in detection rates and simplicity of test coverage. This paper introduces a new approach, called Timeloops, for optimizing system calls in container-based microservices environments. During the startup phase, Timeloops rapidly identifies the system calls a specific application will make and creates a customized filter to discard unnecessary calls. Unlike static analysis-based methods, Timeloops leverages live system information without requiring source code access or manual configuration. Furthermore, Timeloops can adapt to dynamic workloads by periodically refreshing its system call predictions. By optimizing system calls, Timeloops significantly enhances the performance of microservices applications, as evidenced by our experimental results showing substantial speedups when compared to the original Linux system calls. Notably, TimeloLoops achieves a notable average speedup of 2.4X and can save up to 70% of a process's CPU time. Additionally, Timeloops offers a dynamic tracing feature, allowing developers to monitor untrusted services at runtime. Our source code is available online for replication purposes. For a long time, linear classifiers have been extensively studied in Euclidean spaces, 
where their capabilities and efficient algorithms are well understood. However, when we move 
to curved spaces with varying geometries, the complexity of representing and learning 
linear classifiers becomes highly dependent on the local tangent structures of these spaces.

In this work, we explore linear classifiers in generalized curved spaces and establish a 
universal bound on their representability and learnability. Specifically, we define a 
product space of manifold points with Euclidean coordinates and show that, in such a 
space, linear classifiers can be both easily representable and learnable, regardless 
of the curvature of the manifold. Moreover, we prove that this bound is both necessary 
and sufficient, outperforming previous results in certain cases. Furthermore, we identify 
conditions under geometrical structures that facilitate efficient learning of linear classifiers. 

To illustrate the applicability of our findings, we consider two specific product spaces: 
the space of manifold points with Euclidean coordinates and the space of spherical points 
with Euclidean coordinates. In these scenarios, we derive tight bounds on the complexity 
of representing and learning linear classifiers. Ultimately, we highlight the key role 
that local tangent structures play in determining the complexity of learning linear 
classifiers in curved spaces. 

From a practical standpoint, our research has the potential to improve learning linear 
classifiers in manifold-based data, as evidenced by the analysis of a simple example 
in learning linear Hamiltonian classifiers for graph-structured data. 

In terms of future work, our findings suggest several promising research directions, 
including the extension of our results to nonlinear classifiers and the development 
of more efficient algorithms for learning linear classifiers in curved spaces. 

Overall, our goal is to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of learning 
linear classifiers in diverse curved spaces and to facilitate the application of 
our theoretical bounds to such settings. 

Through our research, we aim to bridge the gap between general theoretical results and 
the practical challenges of learning linear classifiers in specific curved spaces, 
with the ultimate objective of gaining insights into the geometric properties of these 
spaces and their implications for learning linear classifiers efficiently. 

To achieve this goal, we plan to investigate various curved spaces, beginning with 
manifolds and spherical spaces, and to examine the potential links between their 
geometric structures and the complexity of learning linear classifiers. 

Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to a more profound understanding of the 
intrinsic complexity of learning linear classifiers in curved spaces and to encourage

The heart of the galaxy, specifically its core, is home to a supermassive black hole that dominates the surrounding environment. As a result, the distribution of nearby stars is influenced by the black hole's gravitational pull, and in some cases, the presence of a bound orbit can be indicated by a distinct break in the luminosity profile. In this study, we examine the effect of a central supermassive black hole on a galaxy with a pre-existing smooth stellar distribution, modeling the star formation process using a hydrodynamic simulation coupled with a semi-analytical galaxy evolution framework. Unlike previous methods, our approach accounts for the dynamic interaction between stars and the growing black hole, allowing us to simulate the evolution of a massive black hole from a low-mass seed to a supermassive state. The resulting data are then analyzed to identify signature patterns that indicate the presence of a central black hole in a galaxy, and we find that a distinct break in the luminosity profile at the core, accompanied by a steep decline in the outer radius, is a distinct characteristic of systems hosting a central black hole. Moreover, we find that a bound orbit can result in the presence of a bright star cluster at the core, and our findings suggest that a supermassive black hole is likely to exist in galaxies exhibiting these features. Conversely, we also identify galaxies with smooth core profiles and no signs of a bound orbit that may still harbor a supermassive black hole, and our research suggests that additional factors, such as a disk/bar potential, could contribute to such a scenario. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights into the complex dynamics of galaxy evolution that can shed light on the co-evolution of black holes and galaxies. In particular, our results imply that a supermassive black hole is likely present in approximately $50\%$ of galaxies with a smooth core and a break in the luminosity profile. In contrast, approximately $30\%$ of galaxies without such a break may still harbor a supermassive black hole, and our findings highlight the need for further investigation into the dynamics of galaxy evolution through high-resolution simulations and observations. A novel method is introduced to enhance entanglement between optical fields and mechanical oscillators in cavity magnomechanics by incorporating a weak convenient coupling. Both quantum and classical fields in the cavity become increasingly intertwined as this coupling strengthens. To achieve this, the quantum mechanical oscillator is driven by a weak coherent force, in addition to being subjected to the influence of the optomechanical coupling. This effect can be observed through the analysis of the covariance matrix of the cavity fields. Notably, the coherent coupling can serve as an effective means of entangling non-conservative systems and may hold significant potential for applications in quantum information processing. Furthermore, the conditions required for its implementation are relatively straightforward to fulfill, making it an attractive option for experiments. The proposed mechanism demonstrates an alternative approach to entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, distinct from traditional methods that rely on strong driving forces. Finally, the feasibility of experimentally observing the entanglement is assessed using realistic parameters derived from state-of-the-art devices. The results indicate that the covariance covariance principle is a viable tool for investigating entanglement in both microscopic and macroscopic systems. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers, relying on the Sun's daily movement to indicate time. This crucial innovation allowed for schedule management, particularly in the classical Islamic era, where the Sun's shadow indicated not only time but also the direction for prayers. Sundials also offered a natural way to divide the day into equal parts, aligning with the needs of prayer times as established by the Prophet Muhammad. Over time, sundials have inspired the development of solar clocks, often featuring innovative and aesthetically pleasing designs. Today, sundials continue to be popular scientific instruments, used to educate people about the Sun's essential characteristics, including its constant radius, angular size, and mean distance from Earth, all of which can be calculated using sundials. By doing so, sundials serve as a natural tool to introduce students and the general public to these fundamental celestial parameters. This article aims to summarize the historical context and scientific applications of sundials, as well as the method for determining the Sun's characteristics using sundials, through the example of a sundial installed at the King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. The study found that the Sundial's data provided results consistent with existing values for the Sun's characteristics, confirming the established values in the International Astronomical Union's fundamental parameters catalog. The results of this research can be utilized for educational purposes, particularly in schools. The study's findings can also be applied to other scientific instruments, such as theocidal clocks and polar clocks, which use the Sun and Moon to indicate time. The main advantage of these instruments is their ability to provide accurate information about the Sun's characteristics, their stability, and the principles of celestial mechanics, all of which can be observed in action. The ocular sundial, in particular, offers a unique opportunity to demonstrate the Sun's characteristics to the general public, particularly its apparent size, which serves as a natural reminder of the Sun's immense size and the principles of celestial physics. This article discusses various types of sundials, their scientific applications, and the benefits they offer to the general public in understanding astronomy. The main advantage of sundials is their ability to indicate time while also educating people about the Sun's characteristics, the principles of celestial mechanics, and the stability of the Sun and the planets, all of which can be observed in action. The study concludes by highlighting the potential of sundials as both timekeepers and educational instruments, used to indicate time and understand the universe, which serves as a natural reminder of the importance of the Sun

vibration of a steel plate struck by a ball. Both experiments yielded detailed, 2D images

performance enhancements in this domain.

system that boasts an exceptional combination of speed, precision, and effectiveness, thus
representing a leading-edge technology in vibrometry analysis.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is at zero temperature. This finding is based on the Schwinger-Feynman gauge choice for gauge dependence, resulting in charge self-interaction that follows from the Ward identities of U(1) symmetry. This interaction is most pronounced at small momentum and frequency transfers. We have used the derived interaction to compute the dynamic density-density correlation under the influence of self-interaction and compared it with a recent experiment. Additionally, we have computed the thermal and quantum fluctuations of this interaction and used them to calculate the specific heat and compressibility of doped graphene. At low temperatures, the specific heat is predicted to behave proportionally to temperature, while the compressibility is linearly related to the doping concentration, displaying a typical steplike behavior. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. Masked Speech Synthesis, a framework that fills in missing speech with synthesized sound, has shown potential in learning contextual representations. However, it requires a substantial amount of labeled data, making it impractical for widespread use. Our solution, Context-Aware Masked Speech Synthesis with Adaptive Masking, addresses these limitations by utilizing both mask and non-masked speech to extract context and adaptively selecting masking methods based on available data. When contextual information is absent, we employ a synthesized speech mask. In contrast, when context is present, we use a transcription mask. Thorough evaluations on three Mandarin speech datasets demonstrate that our system surpasses baseline models in quality and efficiency, requiring no additional labeling. Notably, it exhibits a 50% reduction in masking variability for large datasets, underscoring its ability to adapt masking methods effectively. Recent research has demonstrated that small, carefully crafted input manipulations can deceive a wide range of Deep Neural Networks. Although initial findings were exciting, they also highlighted several limitations, including the requirement for intimate knowledge of the attack model and the target network, as well as the need for numerous attempts to find effective manipulations. In our research, we identify a inherent vulnerability in the architecture of Deep Neural Networks, specifically their expanded layers, which can be exploited by an adversary with limited resources. Our study reveals that these expanded layers generate error-correcting vectors during training, leading to a significant decline in accuracy when confronted with slight input perturbations. Our findings indicate that these error-correcting vectors can be countered through the utilization of a special noise, dubbed the 'anti-noise', which substantially boosts the network's resilience to attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these anti-noises can be incorporated into the training process as an regularization layer, significantly enhancing the network's robustness with only a minor reduction in performance. Our proposed approach is validated through experiments on various attack methods, including targeted and untargeted attacks, across multiple datasets and network architectures. Our findings indicate that this method is effective in improving the robustness of DNNs, particularly when compared to existing defense mechanisms. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of error-correcting capabilities in the expanded layers of DNNs, which could have implications for the design of more secure and resilient deep neural networks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharif9/anti-noise.

A solar type-I noise storm is an extremely intense and variable continuum emission observed around chromospheric footpoints of flaring loops. This phenomenon is highly correlated with metric burst radio waves and varies significantly in different storms. We investigated a solar type-I noise storm associated with a microflare observed on AR12671. The storm, present in data from Ooty Radio Telescope at 30 MHz, shows a clear increase in intensity from December 13 to 14, 2022. The storm's source parameters, including spectral indices and flux densities, experienced two distinct phases of evolution: steady and dynamic changes. During the impulsive phase of the microflare, the source exhibited a shift in location and variable behavior in its 30 MHz emission. The source's behavior in the post-flare period showed increasing complexity and variability, along with a rise in its 30 MHz emission. Analysis of the Caltech Big Bear Vacuum Telescope observations revealed that the storm's radio source overlapped with the moving footpoints of the flaring loops, indicating their association with the microflare. The variable source parameters in the storm suggest multiple energy release episodes and/or changes in electron beam properties. The storm's behavior can be understood through models of interacting plasma processes and/or energy deposition sites, which can provide further clarity on its phenomena. Further research is needed to comprehend the storm's underlying physical processes. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity. Furthermore, the application of a differential pressure gauge allowed for the accurate measurement of the trap's vapor pressure, confirming the efficiency of the integrated MOT system. This innovative design is expected to contribute to the development of more portable and versatile trapping technologies. Additionally, the MOT's cold atomic sample can be utilized for the study of low-velocity atomic emissions, which has potential applications in the detection of dark matter. Finally, the integrated MOT architecture presents an opportunity for the creation of a portable and versatile quantum memory, enabling the investigation of the relationship between spin and momentum. One of the earliest applications of neural networks was automatic colorization of grayscale images. While early models achieved this task, they struggled with other complex image transformation tasks. Recent breakthroughs, however, have enabled automatic colorization with impressive results, but the underlying mechanisms of these models remain difficult to interpret. A new method is proposed, using a framework that separates color and image creation to improve the overall visual quality and achieve more realistic results. The framework consists of two stages: first, a learned generator produces a base grayscale image; second, a learned colorizer applies a set of color gradients to this base image, effectively "painting" it. Through this divide-and-conquer approach, each stage can be optimized independently, resulting in more balanced and detailed colors, along with improved image structure, as demonstrated by the high resolution used in this study. The proposed method significantly surpasses previous techniques in automatic colorization, according to the widely used FRECHL scores, while also being more efficient to train and requiring less memory. Notably, when applied to grayscale images, the method produces high-quality colorized results, but also reveals a base grayscale image, often nearly original. This property enables the discovery of existing images that were previously enhanced during training or through post-processing, as shown in the provided supplementary video. The method is implemented in a GAN framework, specifically in the SPECTRANalyzer network, but can be adapted to other GAN-based image-to-image transformation tasks by separating color and image creation. We've developed a novel numerical scheme for determining Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on differentiable activation functions, enabling the computation of weights through a smooth transformation of the input data. This weight calculation is grounded in a generalization of the Spectral Embedding Theorem and can be efficiently computed using spectral graph polynomials, whose smooth approximation is based on Gaussian Hermite polynomials, allowing for an effective trade-off between accuracy and smoothness. This approach has been successfully tested on various synthetic and real-world datasets and compares favorably to established ANNs, including those using stochastic gradient descent, in terms of predictive performance. Furthermore, when applied to graph data, our method has outperformed or matched the performance of numerous graph deep learning benchmarks, such as those employing gradient-based ANNs, graph convolutional networks, and graph attention networks, across various benchmarks such as BioGRID, BioGRID2, and ogbn-arxiv. Notably, our method has achieved superior results on the ogbn-amazon670 dataset in a competition against 160+ teams. Additionally, our method has demonstrated promising performance on various image recognition tasks, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet, when compared to 150+ other approaches. Overall, our approach represents a significant advancement in the design of efficient and accurate ANNs, and it has been made available on our website at https://mattmahoney.net/anngp.html. You can also download the code from https://github.com/mattmahoney/anngp. Additionally, the weights for all experiments can be found at https://mattmahoney.net/anngp_weights.html. Finally, a video explaining our work can be accessed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Q4fXOvF7oE. In conclusion, our numerical scheme for computing ANN weights offers an attractive balance of efficiency, accuracy, and smoothness, making it an attractive choice for a wide range of machine learning applications. This is particularly important in light of the recently demonstrated adversarial vulnerabilities of many deep learning models, as smooth weights can be more resistant to such attacks; see, for example, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16667. In Tb3RuO7, a phase transition occurs at 15 K, where the magnetic structures of two ruthenium sublattices change from a simple tetragonal arrangement to a more complex one with intertwined patterns. In our work, we present an MLP architecture that can be trained end-to-end to extract general, dual-purpose features from data, which can then be utilized for both image and video processing applications. This approach enables the shared features to be adapted to a specific task only after being acquired through joint training on multiple tasks. In our evaluations, the proposed method demonstrated superior performance in both still images and video processing, outperforming other compared methods. Additionally, the study highlights the benefits of dual-MLP networks in terms of reduced complexity, training efficiency, and faster task adaptation. You can find the code implementation at https://github.com/basilevh/dual-mlp.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific examples, such as de Sitter spaces and anti-de Sitter spaces, have their momentum operators explicitly defined and associated with the conformal group structure. Furthermore, the connection between these momentum operators and the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter algebras is clarified, demonstrating that not all de Sitter and anti-de Sitter algebras arise from Killing momentum operators. Additionally, the concept of covariant derivative killing vector fields is investigated, revealing that only flat manifolds, including those with a compact structure in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7, have such vector fields with their covariant derivative vanishing. This leads to the discovery that constant mean curvature manifolds do not admit momentum operators in the form of Killing vector fields. Lastly, momentum operators defined through geodesic flow are identified and related to the Liouville vector fields, with their properties, such as action on differential forms, being examined. The findings show that for manifolds with a compact structure, the momentum operators defined through geodesic flow fail to satisfy the Killing condition, except in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. This research provides an extensive characterization of momentum operators on intrinsically curved manifolds, covering various geometric, algebraic, and dynamical aspects. It also identifies remaining open questions for potential future investigation. Two appendices are included to provide supplementary material, including a proof of a Schr\"{o}dinger type identity and the demonstration of differential forms' invariance under conformal transformations.}

Despite their widespread reach, such content is often marred by inaccuracies, with severe consequences in critical areas like public health and politics. Existing fact-checking endeavors are hindered by limited scope, primarily focusing on prominent platforms and languages. To expand their reach, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a social media aggregator to tap into a diverse range of content in multiple languages, labeling each with crowd-sourced factual annotations. Building upon this dataset, we establish a competition where machine learning models can be developed to tackle the intricate task of fact-checking. The competition showcases substantial progress, highlighting the potential of large-scale, multi-language fact-checking, and we anticipate it will foster continued advancements in this vital area. The resulting dataset and competition code are publicly accessible at https://www.grasp-lab.org/socialfact.

A powerful new tool has been introduced for analyzing cosmic structures and their inherent properties, the weighted skew-spectrum, which has shown superior performance in extracting information compared to traditional power-spectra. This skew-spectrum can be applied across various phenomena, including galaxy clustering, cosmic shear, and intensity mapping, by utilizing weighted counts of galaxy or pixel data based on their angular or redshift separation. This technique has been successfully tested on data from the SDSS, with simulations demonstrating its ability to accurately predict N-body simulations and outperform power-spectra analysis in retrieving parameters such as the matter density and primordial power-spectra index. Furthermore, SKP-spectra have been found to be more sensitive to bias and shot noise than power-spectra, highlighting their potential to provide unbiased estimates of these parameters. This new approach has great promise for future surveys like Euclid, LSST, and the Stage-IV prime focus instruments, where it may provide essential information for cosmological parameter estimation. A Python package, called SKP-spectra, has been developed to facilitate the analysis and is available for public use at [https://github.com/ash3m/skpspectra](https://github.com/ash3m/skpspectra). Both packages are updateable to reflect the latest simulations and can be easily customized for application to new data sets. This research demonstrates the potential of skew-spectra to revolutionize the analysis of future cosmological surveys, offering a more precise and sensitive method for extracting information and making accurate predictions. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we have developed a novel approach to creating robust models that can effectively handle real-world uncertainties. This methodology involves training Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) using perturbation-based adversarial training, which can be realized through the integration of a uncertainty-aware loss function and a reinforcement mechanism that promotes diversity in the uncertainty-related loss imposed on the network during training. This method has been successfully tested on various standard benchmarks and compared to established robust training techniques, with the results indicating a significant improvement in adversarially trained BNNs' robustness under both deterministic and stochastic perturbations. Furthermore, the benefits of this approach extend to the network's generalization performance, with the BNNs exhibiting enhanced out-of-distribution detection capabilities. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/Chen-Ethan/BAT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01283

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences, also fueling widespread online rumors that further exacerbated public panic. This study aimed to understand the dynamics of rumor dissemination by analyzing the relationship between emotional cues, sentiment propagation, and rumor spread. A methodology combining machine learning and network analysis was employed to examine a dataset of Weibo posts containing emotional language. The results revealed that emotional cues are transmitted from individuals with strong sentiments, creating clusters of like-minded groups, which often serve as echo chambers, amplifying rumors. Furthermore, rumors are more likely to spread when linked to popular topics, especially those related to public health and government responses. The research identified several key factors contributing to rumor dissemination, including social connections, group affiliations, and the presence of 'rumor seeders.' The findings provide insights for mitigating the spread of online rumors during future public health crises by targeting these factors. Additionally, the study's methodologies can be applied to other social media platforms to analyze emotional sentiment propagation. This research examines the effectiveness of dimensionality reduction methods in hyperspectral pixel classification, utilizing compression ratios instead of feature count. Fifteen methods were tested, along with three pixel classification algorithms, and the findings were analyzed through a comprehensive statistical assessment. The findings reveal that certain techniques, such as PCA-LLE, UMAP, and t-SNE, yield high classification accuracies even at aggressive compression rates. A novel approach is introduced to assess the feasibility of using a method at a particular compression rate, taking into account both accuracy and stability. This metric can serve as a guide in choosing optimal dimensionality reduction methods for hyperspectral pixel classification tasks. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they come with a significant cost. The idea of the lottery ticket hypothesis suggests that within a pre-trained network, there is a smaller sub-network that can be trained alone to achieve similar or often better performance in a target task. Our research focuses on exploring the existence of this trainable sub-network within a pre-trained convolutional network in the context of image classification. We identify that a randomly sampled sub-network is unlikely to exist within a pre-trained convolutional network and that a sub-network requiring adversarial data augmentation does not exist either. We then develop an innovative and efficient approach to find a trainable sub-network without an extensive search process by incorporating evolutionary algorithms to optimize weights as well as module selection within the pre-trained network. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a sub-network can be obtained which can perform well on the target task without needing the original full network. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a critical decision, with numerous loss functions having different training and generalization outcomes. Previous studies have started uncovering the reasons behind this variation in behavior. In this research, we examine how the structure of a classification task influences the performance of a deep neural network when trained using different loss functions. By doing so, we identified both numerical and categorical features present in the CIFAR-100 dataset, which revealed how various loss functions extract distinct visual cues from the images. Furthermore, we discovered that a soft-hardness paradigm can be employed to determine an optimal loss function for a particular classification task. Based on our findings, PPO has been demonstrated to effectively optimize loss function choices, even in the absence of label information. Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of loss function design in deep neural networks and provides a framework for future exploration in this domain. Finally, the optical absorption spectrum of the system is also examined, revealing distinct features in the insulating phase compared to the semimetallic state. the overall volume of music. This research examined loudness in detail, discovering
a significant increase in the complexity of songs over time and two distinct
patterns: a gradual shift from the 1960s to the 2000s and a sudden change in the
1980s. To understand which artists contributed to these changes, we analyzed the
volume of prominent rock bands. Additionally, we found that songs produced by
professional composers for film followed a different pattern, and we explored how
these findings correlated with the development of the music industry during that
time period. It was discovered that successful rock bands of the 1970s and 1980s were
producing music with unique characteristics that deviated from the typical
dynamics. Furthermore, we found that there was a significant disparity between the
music generated by humans and computers, specifically the songs in the Jukebox
Algorithms dataset, revealing distinct patterns in each. This research sheds
light on the creative influence of technology on music generation. Lastly, to
determine the extent to which a particular genre is responsible for the changes
in music, we analyzed the songs in the Million Song Dataset using the audio features
of jazz, classical, and hip-hop music, and found that hip-hop, which emerged in the
1970s, had a significant impact on the changes in music over time. To visualize the
evolution of music, we created a dynamic audio visualization that displays the
volume of music and shows the changes in the characteristics of music over time.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the computational lambda calculus. When this harmony condition is applied to cut-elimination theorems in intuitionistic natural deduction, it yields a more straightforward proof that does not rely on the recovery principle. Furthermore, by translating harmony into a cut-admissible rule, a normalized cut-elimination procedure can be derived for intuitionistic natural deduction, analogous to the computational cut-elimination theorem. Finally, this paper provides cut-elimination theorems for classical natural deduction by combining two independent harmony conditions, one for \lnot and one for \vee, and also investigates the possibility of a unified harmony for both, although this proves more complicated to formulate. Cut-elimination theorems for classical natural deduction can further be generalized into a harmony-based, harmony-inductive cut-elimination theorem that accommodates additional operators such as \bot,!, and?, by defining a unified harmony for all involved rules. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. This novel approach not only optimizes learned rewards but also rectifies biases in agents' policies, all without necessitating access to optimal action outcomes. To facilitate region identification on complex state spaces, we employ interactive tools, allowing human labelers to label compact representations of trajectories and dynamically adjust the display based on their inputs. This approach proves scalable in that it is adaptable to various dimensionality reductions and allows multiple labelers to contribute by labeling separate segments, thereby facilitating collaborative learning. Moreover, we demonstrate that our method can be modified to engage labelers in more intricate comparative tasks, such as ranking, to improve the learning of comparative preferences, a potentially valuable application. To implement this novel human feedback method, we designed a user-friendly web interface using three.js and a backend based on Flask, allowing seamless communication between the client and server, and making it easy to customize the visualization and add more interactive features. This approach effectively integrates human feedback into reward learning, as evidenced by our experiments on basic Mujoco tasks, where we show that even small amounts of labeling data can enhance the performance of learning agents, often surpassing that of agents trained without human feedback. We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points. The development of robust tools for tracking vortex loops enables the computation of statistics for generic diffeomorphism orbits, notably demonstrating that the orbit's volume shrinks exponentially over time. Additionally, we identify a transition in statistical behavior, linking it to the point vortex case for high vorticity levels. The methods employed are versatile and can be applied to other types of singular vorticities, such as those associated with rigid bodies in wave-free regions. This paper builds upon the established connections between Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimators, particularly Average Treatment Effect through Propensity Score (AIPW) and its non-parametric variant (nAIPW), in the context of causal inference. It's established that both AIPW and nAIPW satisfy double robustness, causal path, and local rank conditions. Under causal assumptions, both estimators converge uniformly to the true ATE. The paper introduces a general framework for establishing uniform convergence of ATE estimators and uses this framework to demonstrate the consistency of several high-dimensional ATE estimators. This framework can also be applied to establish the consistency of several doubly robust estimators. The findings are further illustrated with consistent estimators for the conditional treatment effect. The proposed theory is validated through empirical analysis of real-world data from studies on the effectiveness of direct-to-consumer advertising on prescription medications and treatment outcomes in clinical trials. The study demonstrates that nAIPW performs comparably to AIPW, particularly in complex scenarios involving multiple treatments. Our research reveals that in the context of $Q$ learning, even with the assumption that the adversary only modifies a limited number of data entries, it becomes significantly more complex to create a robust algorithm compared to what has been traditionally believed. Specifically, we demonstrate that any learning algorithm that can resist adversarial manipulation in the offline setting requires at least a much larger sample size, one that grows linearly with the size of the state and action spaces, as opposed to a polynomial growth. This finding applies to settings where the rewards and transitions in the interaction follow a uniform distribution over the samples, but our result may be limited to non-uniform distributions. Moreover, we show that by assuming that the underlying MDP is structured, with the adversary aiming to mislead the learner, it becomes possible to create learning algorithms that can resist the effect of the adversary's manipulation with a sample size that grows sublinearly. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - when handling background, semantic, and adversarial shifts, which are commonly encountered in real-world scenarios. In our study, each type of shift was examined using multiple datasets, and the results revealed that density estimation is more effective in identifying background and adversarial shifts, whereas model calibration excels in detecting semantic shifts. Furthermore, a combination of both methods did not consistently improve performance compared to using each method individually. The findings of our study could facilitate the development of more effective detection methods for out-of-distribution examples and highlight the need for a standardized classification system for different types of shifts. In this study, we explore the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible pairs of elements in a universe of size n, where each element is associated with a value from the set {0, 1,..., f-1}. This leads to the definition of an $f$-convolution of two functions $p$ and $q$ defined on this universe, where each pair $(x, y)$ receives a value equal to $p(x) \cdot q(y)$ if $x$ is not equal to $y$. This concept is further generalized to the parallel version of convolution, where for each $k$ from $0$ to $f-1$, all pairs $(x, y)$ where $x+y \equiv k \mod f$ receive the value $p(x) \cdot q(y)$. We examine the brute-force approach for computing the convolution, resulting in a time complexity of $\Theta(n^2)$. Additionally, when $f$ is equal to or greater than $n$, we propose a randomized reduction that solves the problem in $O(f \log f + np)$ time, where the value of $p$ is unknown in advance. We explore the deterministic version of this reduction, resulting in a time complexity of $O(np + \min\{n, \sqrt{f}\} p)$. This study further delves into the parallel version of convolution, revealing a time complexity of $\Theta(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})$ for $f$ and $n$ in the range of $\Omega( \sqrt{n})$ to $\tilde{O}(n)$ and $p$ being a small constant. We explore the application of our findings to the parallel version of convolution, resulting in a time complexity of $O(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})$ for $f$ and $n$ in the range of $\Omega( \sqrt{n})$ to $\tilde{O}(n)$ and $p$ being a small constant. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its properties. We've conducted new high-resolution spectroscopy using the ESPaDOnS instrument at the CFHT, along with re-analysing archival data from the Keck II NIR spectrograph. The analysis employs a cutting-edge atmospheric model that allows for optimal fitting. Our estimates for GJ 229B's mass and effective temperature are 107.0 +/- 3.0 MJ and 722 +/- 20 K, respectively. We've also compared these values with previous spectroscopic estimates, finding substantial discrepancies. Notably, our study confirms the presence of methane and water in GJ 229B's atmosphere, with further evidence supporting the presence of aerosols at least one km above the atmosphere's base pressure level. Our data show that GJ 229B's velocity is consistent with a low-eccentricity orbit around its parent star, with a velocity variation of 3.0 km/s over its 88-day orbit and no evidence of a velocity difference of of 13 km/s as previously suggested. Our findings suggest that planetary disturbance is unlikely to have significantly affected the atmosphere of GJ 229B, with the possibility that late-type T-dwarfs may be susceptible to similar atmospheric modifications by planetary bodies. We've released our new data into the public domain for further use.

To search for the potential existence of the exotic $0^{--}$ state, we investigated the ${D^*^2}$ process at proton-proton collision energy of 5, 7, 8.5 and 13 TeV within the framework of $t$-channel, assuming it as a $0^{--}$ resonance. Notably, the data on $\rho$ and $\rho\pi$ systems, obtained from LHCb experiments at different energy levels, did not demonstrate clear evidence for the resonance, and we concluded that the information available is sufficient to indicate the exclusion of the $t$-channel model at a confidence level of 88\% and 95% for the energy ranges of 5-8.5 GeV and 13 GeV, respectively. Furthermore, we proposed an $S$-channel model for the process ${D^*^2}\to \rho^{0}(i^+ {J\!/\!ψ)}$, where the latter two particles are produced back-to-back, and we found that this model can account for the experimentally observed rates at 5 and 7 TeV with an acceptable fit quality. Importantly, our study reveals that the $S$-channel model predicts a broad resonance with the same quantum numbers as the $T$ state at around 2.82 GeV, and we suggested that this resonance may potentially correspond to the observed candidates at 2.82 GeV, and also to the $T$ state reported by LUS, based on the available data at 13 TeV. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult task, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous approaches have employed diverse representation types, yet overlooked the benefits of retaining environmental information for future use.
We introduce MemoNav, a novel memory-based image-goal navigation framework, which builds upon existing experiences to maintain a working memory of environmental cues.
MemoNav leverages a contrasting loss to preserve information in working memory and a common loss for the main network, thereby retaining short-term memory and discarding irrelevant details.
Through retrospective viewing, MemoNav recurrently updates its working memory as it approaches closer to the destination, demonstrating superior performance in goal-conditioning and memory utilization compared to prior methods. Additionally, we highlight the system's ability to rectify previous errors by revising past working memories. Experimental results show MemoNav's capacity to correct navigational mistakes and maintain a dynamic environmental memory, which is visually verified. The code is available at https://github.com/alexeygogel/MemoNav.

However, several applications need even more licensed spectrum than what cellular networks offer. To supply additional spectrum, wireless communication systems can utilize unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz band for LTE-U/LTE-D2D, and 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi 6E, with hidden Wi-Fi risk due to unexpected interference. To mitigate interference and ensure fair coexistence between cellular and Wi-Fi when deploying these technologies, the industry consensus is to employ the IEEE 802.11bf standard, with the exact methods and techniques yet to be determined. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach based on stochastic control to mitigate interference and maintain fair coexistence between cellular/LTE-D2D and Wi-Fi, with the objective of obtaining the optimal online algorithm before knowing the future processes. The proposed algorithm is adapted from a known optimal offline algorithm for a similar model and is demonstrated to be the best among all online algorithms in simulations, with performance just 1.12 times that of the optimal cellular/LTE-D2D spectrum efficiency achieved when knowing the future processes in advance. Also, the proposed algorithm is shown to be better than two other known online algorithms in simulations, with superior cellular/LTE-D2D spectrum efficiency. We have developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we have detailed two specific cases, focusing on synchronization in phase oscillators and the spread of epidemic dynamics within a population. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we presented simulations to illustrate a hypothetical scenario of synchronization-induced epidemic control. This framework can be expanded to model various processes and we intend to explore more applications in future research. A associated software is available online at https://hypgraph.gitub.io/ for use in simulating dynamical processes on hypergraphs. The source code can be accessed through the HypGraph repository on GitHub at https://github.com/HypGraph/HypGraph.git. The package includes a range of features such as graph generation, weight assignment, and dynamic process definition, enabling users to model different scenarios. The HypGraph library supports Python 3.7 and later versions. A step-by-step guide to using the software can be found in the User Guide available online at https://hypgraph.gitub.io/user-guide. The authors welcome user feedback and suggestions for future improvements, which can be provided through the issue tracker at https://github.com/HypGraph/HypGraph/issues. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly linked $\alpha$ particles at $E_{\mathrm{exc}} \approx 7.65$ MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has long been debated. The Hoyle state primarily decays through a direct route or indirectly via the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ ground state. The relative significance of the direct decay is often interpreted as an indicator of the $\alpha$-condensate nature of the state. The problem with studying the Hoyle state decay lies in the detection of the decay products, particularly the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ ground state, which is hidden beneath the Fe background at the target end. A new experiment was conducted at the iRAS facility using a 120$^\circ$ angular separation between the target and the particle detector to analyze the indirect decay of the Hoyle state. The results show that the corrected ratio of direct to indirect decays is approximately 0.944, which supports the idea that the Hoyle state consists of highly linked $\alpha$ particles. The experimental results agree with the findings of a previous study at Gazelle, and the observation of a significant change in the decay channel from indirect to direct as one ascends in excitation in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ provides valuable insights into the evolution of the isoteric yield in the region of the Rydberg matter. The study conducted at the IRAS facility provides novel evidence that the Hoyle state is an $\alpha$-condensate rather than a compact $\alpha$ cluster. The findings of this research are important for the understanding of the $\alpha$-condensate phenomenon and may be applied to other systems such as $^{16}$O and $^{20}$Ne in their respective energy domains. The study paves the way for further theoretical and experimental investigations into the $\alpha$-condensate phenomenon at the many-body level. Significant breakthroughs have been made in the study of dynamic fracture in two-dimensional brittle materials, but an in-depth understanding of the instability mechanisms of cracks moving at high speeds remains lacking. Through three-dimensional numerical simulations, we have gained insight into the oscillatory instability of cracks in two different materials: one with a rigid line and another with a cohesive zone. Our findings reveal that in the first material, the instability is solely caused by the interaction between stress waves, whereas in the second material, the emergence of oscillations relies on the loss of cohesion behind the crack tip. Our results also show that the peak frequency of oscillations is related to the material's elastic properties and that the amplitude decays due to the loss of energy. However, in certain cases, the decay can be slowed by the loss of cohesion. Our research provides a foundation for the understanding of crack instability in three-dimensional dynamic fracture. Furthermore, the results have implications for the analysis of two-dimensional numerical simulations, highlighting the need to verify that such simulations accurately captures the physics of crack oscillations. Finally, the study has practical applications in predicting and controlling the stability of crack propagation in various engineering materials. In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with state information available to the transmitter and receiver. Our investigation focuses on the optimal performance limits of these channels given different assumptions about the availability and use of this state information. Specifically, we consider three distinct scenarios: when no state information is utilized, when it is available but remains unknown to the receiver, and when both the transmitter and receiver have access to it. Our analysis reveals that when state information is available to at least one of the two, a single communication session may be sufficient to achieve the optimal transmission rate, whereas in the absence of state information, these channels are classified as feedback-stable or unstable, depending on their characteristics. Our findings are supported by several examples that illustrate the differences between these cases and also demonstrate the existence of channels requiring multiple communication sessions to reach the optimal transmission rate. Moreover, we identify a subclass of feedback-stable channels, referred to as unifying channels, for which a single communication session is sufficient to reach the optimal transmission rate. Our study further shows that unifying channels can be characterized by a specific property in stable channels and, as a special case, includes all stable channels, along with binary memoryless channels and certain types of partial feedback channels. Our work also sheds light on the distinct roles played by state information at the transmitter and receiver, demonstrating that when state information is available only to the receiver, it is possible to require an infinite number of communication sessions to reach the optimal transmission rate, even if state information is available to the transmitter. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the number of communication sessions required in feedback-stable channels. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of state information and feedback in achieving optimal transmission rates for these channels. They also highlight the significance of distinguishing between different assumptions about state information availability in analyzing these channels. Our study opens up avenues for future research, particularly in characterizing feedback-stable channels and identifying all feasible transmission strategies for these channels. Additionally, we explore the possibility of relaxing the requirement of knowing the current state at both the transmitter and receiver while maintaining a bounded number of communication sessions to reach the optimal transmission rate. This study tackles the challenge of verifying factual claims related to tabular data by introducing two core sub-tasks: "Factual Consistency" and "Comparability". Factual Consistency involves identifying discrete data cells that contradict a claim when it's false. Comparability, on the other hand, requires pinpointing data cells that would support a claim if true or know its correct value. We present comprehensive benchmarks for these sub-tasks across English and Chinese languages, drawing from existing datasets and creating new ones from scratch. To address this problem, we also introduce the first wave of machine learning models capable of extracting data cells from tables. Our findings reveal that Factual Consistency is more feasible than Comparability but also underscore the need for more refined models. Additionally, we discover that Factual Consistency in Chinese can be significantly more challenging than in English due to differences in data presentation. The full code and dataset are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ai4society/TABLES-ML. To facilitate future research, we also establish a benchmarking platform for evaluating models on these tasks at: https://eval.ai/competition/tables-ml. This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and addressing potential counterarguments to these justifications. Additionally, it investigates alternative interpretations of Quantum Mechanics that are formulated using real numbers. Since the problem of measurement is particularly challenging for real-time formulations, our examination focuses on a distinct approach, the real-Gelfand-Mazur theorem, to demonstrate the inherent need for complex numbers in one aspect of Quantum Mechanics, the representation of projective states. This study aims to provide a clear understanding of the reasons behind the widespread adoption of complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

The gradient of pressure $\nababla p$ is calculated by differentiating the pressure function $p(r,\phi)$ with respect to $r$ and $\phi$. The resulting velocity vector is then used to determine the mass flow rate per unit width $Q$ by integrating the velocity component tangential to the contour curve. The contour curve is defined by the equation $r = a e^{b \phi}$, and the integration is performed over the angle $\phi$ from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. The solution involves a change of variables and the application of a gamma function to evaluate the integral. The mass flow rate per unit width $Q$ is found to be $Q = \frac{3 \pi \alpha^2 P_0}{2b^3}$. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper presents a detailed analysis of various communication techniques that can efficiently utilize multiple cores for neural network simulations on a guest system, resulting in a substantial performance boost during testing. By combining the best communication methods, the simulation's throughput increased by 97%, outperforming existing solutions in the field. This improvement enables the testing of complex neural networks on neuromorphic architectures, which was previously not possible at such a scale. Furthermore, the knowledge gained from this research can be applied to other types of system simulations, such as ASICs, where similar communication challenges arise during testing. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into a
clear, logical argument that can be applied to other reasoning systems. In this
context, Indecision Trees are positioned as a form of abstract, logical tree
structure adapted for use in a specific, real-world problem. The study compares
Indecision Trees to existing models such as Decision Trees, Random Forest, and
XGBoost using data from the Kaggle's COVID19 challenge. The results indicate that
Indecision Trees achieve comparable accuracy to these models but possess the
ability to be interpreted through a series of logical premises that can be used
for explanations, training other agents, or transferring knowledge to other
reasoning systems. Furthermore, a demonstration is provided of how
Indecision Trees can be utilized in a group of autonomous agents, each utilizing its
own learned tree structure, to make collective decisions based on individual
agency. The study shows that these autonomous agents can reach a joint decision
faster than if each took an individual, isolated approach. The code for

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across various domains, but its computation can be hindered by the O(N^2) complexity of time series, making it impractical for large datasets. To overcome this limitation, recent research introduced PrunedDTW, a fast and accurate variant with a reduced complexity of O(N alpha), where alpha is the alignment length. While PrunedDTW outperforms traditional DTW in terms of time efficiency, it compromises some accuracy. To build upon this work, our proposed EAPrunedDTW algorithm further refines PrunedDTW by utilizing early average acceleration to significantly reduce alpha, thereby improving accuracy while maintaining or surpassing the speed of PrunedDTW. The enhanced accuracy of EAPrunedDTW is demonstrated through the comparison of stroke representation using our approach against PrunedDTW and DTW in multiple tasks, including handwriting similarity assessment and stroke segmentation. Furthermore, the source code of EAPrunedDTW is available at https://github.com/ChenXinyu1998/EAPrunedDTW for public use. The experimental results reveal that EAPrunedDTW offers a good balance of speed and accuracy, making it a suitable alternative to DTW for time series analysis in various applications. The accuracy and precision of EAPrunedDTW are assessed through the calculation of the precision of optimal alignments and the comparison with ground truth. The computational efficiency of EAPrunedDTW is validated by measuring its runtime on multiple hardware configurations, including a high-performance GPU. The effectiveness of EAPrunedDTW in time series analysis is evaluated through multiple tasks, including the classification of handwritten digits, stroke representation, and segmentation, which demonstrate its capability to produce accurate results on large datasets. The potential of EAPrunedDTW to be integrated into deep neural networks is explored by integrating it with a handwritten digit classification task, revealing the potential for a significant increase in accuracy. The integration of EAPrunedDTW with deep neural networks shows promising results, with the potential for future research to further improve its performance, and we anticipate it will also be useful for other time series analysis tasks. Current educational methods are inadequate, failing to effectively teach testing concepts to novice programmers. These concepts are crucial for writing high-quality code, but traditional approaches often leave students under-prepared, resulting in poorly written tests and extended debugging times. To address this issue, a novel educational resource, the Testing Instructor's Guide, has been developed to provide an effective framework for incorporating inquiry-based learning techniques. Comprising a set of pre-designed, thought-provoking prompts and model lesson plans featuring real coding examples, the guide equips instructors with the tools to guide students through a deeper exploration of testing fundamentals. By utilizing the Testing Instructor's Guide, instructors can create customized learning experiences that stimulate student reflection, foster critical thinking, and build a more in-depth understanding of testing principles. To support continued improvement and dissemination, an associated website has been established, offering additional resources, including a repository of instructor-submitted lesson plans and an invitation for the community to contribute their own teaching approaches. Ultimately, the goal of the Testing Instructor's Guide is to empower instructors to experiment with various teaching methods, exchange knowledge, and collectively develop effective educational strategies for teaching testing concepts. By doing so, the project aims to contribute meaningfully to the educational community and continue evolving to meet the changing needs of novice programmers, who are increasingly encouraged to engage in areas like data science, artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things. To facilitate ongoing development and community engagement, the project is committed to remaining flexible and adaptable in response to emerging trends and ideas in computer science education. By fostering a collaborative and continuous improvement process, the project aspires to create a lasting impact on the educational strategies of instructors and, by extension, the skills and knowledge of novice programmers. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods. However, standard visualization techniques often fall short due to their inability to effectively convey complex, high-dimensional data or provide a comprehensive understanding of a model's decision-making processes. This study presents a novel, immersive 3D visual framework for exploring the internal workings of a black-box classifier. By utilizing an interactive, immersive environment, this approach enables the identification of critical features and bounds on feature values that contribute to a positive classification outcome. The effectiveness of this method was demonstrated in a classification task involving a simulated medical imaging scenario, where it successfully revealed key features underlying the decision-making process. Additionally, this study highlights potential future applications of this immersive XAI framework in various domains. Although feature modification is part of the proposed system, its primary focus lies in using immersive XAI for educational purposes or understanding counterfactual scenarios, rather than actual feature manipulation. Furthermore, the study notes that finding the optimal feature values for a positive classification outcome may not necessarily correspond to the actual feature values used by the classifier, often due to the over-smoothing or local maximization issues inherent in gradient-based methods. As such, it recommends using the identified feature ranges rather than specific values for further analysis or feature adjustment. Overall, this immersive XAI framework offers a versatile tool for comprehensive system training, informed feature manipulation, and decision-making feature selection across a wide range of applications. The study's findings are available for reproduction through an online demo URL and can be accessed via the repository linked in the text. Additionally, the used technology has minimal hardware and software requirements, allowing its integration into existing systems with minimal additional costs. As such, this immersive XAI framework presents an efficient and adaptable solution for the explanation of black-box classifiers in various domains. The study suggests several promising avenues for future research, including the application of this immersive XAI framework to models capable of generating counterfactual explanations, an in-depth comparison with other visual XAI approaches, and an exploration of how this immersive XAI framework could be utilized for the classification of graphs, which presents an intriguing challenge for future work. The integration of immersive XAI with active learning presents another promising area of research, where identifying key features and decision-making factors could aid in the selection of informative samples for model refinement. Moreover, Graph Convolutional Networks are found to enter a state of saturation, and their final hidden layer is universally similar to a global vector, regardless of the network's architecture. This universal characteristic of Graph Convolutional Networks can be exploited to perform efficient multi-task training. Unlike Neural Networks, which become increasingly complex, Graph Convolutional Networks are found to demonstrate a straightforward and predictable pattern of improvement in their performance as they get larger. We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. Specifically, the functions are linked to interactions defined by $M$ and $N$-spin vectors, where $M$ is associated with the movement and $N$ is associated with the direction of parton movement in the transverse direction. Notably, the functions are part of a broader class that includes the Sivers function, and we draw a parallel between them to illustrate how they are linked to the movement of partons, as well as their respective functions with spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. These functions can be studied in deep inelastic scattering experiments involving leptons and nuclei, particularly in the measurement of spin-dependent azimuthal distributions of hadrons. Furthermore, we examine the functions' accessibility in experiments using various nuclei such as $^4$He and $^{56}$Fe. Additionally, we discuss the functions' measurements in the context of SIDIS and $e^-$$e^+$ collisions. Moreover, we explore the functions' connections to the parton Sodded-Matted effect and parton spin-Matted effect in both SIDIS and $e^-$$e^+$ collisions. Lastly, we reflect on how these functions can be measured and their implications on our understanding of parton distribution functions can be explored using various probes in both SIDIS and $e^-$$e^+$ collisions. \end{abstract}

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, allowing the creation of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing the need for sophisticated surface preparation techniques. By combining this technique with chemical epitaxy, it may be possible to grow Heusler compounds - a group of alloys with unique properties and wide-ranging applications - on graphene. To investigate this potential, we employed Auger electron spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to analyze a experiment involving the growth of Co2FeP and Co2MnSi alloys on graphene. Our results show distinct changes in the electron spectra as the materials are grown under different conditions, indicating the presence of chemical elements. However, further examination using Raman spectroscopy and low-energy electron diffraction reveals that the materials do not exhibit epitaxial growth - rather, they form randomly on the graphene surface. Notably, our findings suggest the presence of graphene compounds with chemical compositions, but these are distinct from the intended Heusler compounds. This research highlights the need for more sophisticated analysis to confirm remote epitaxy and chemical compounds in the future. Ultimately, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the remote epitaxy process and the challenges associated with chemical epitaxy. It is hoped that these findings will inspire the development of improved techniques for the remote epitaxy of materials with chemical properties. Recent advancements in powerful telescopes have enabled the identification of massive galaxy clusters through the observation of multiply lensed galaxies at distant ages. By studying these clusters, scientists can better understand the structure of galaxy clusters and their surrounding environment. A new discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope reveals four strongly lensed galaxies within the galaxy cluster glgC-1 at a redshift of 0.40. These galaxies form the core of a giant elliptical galaxy that is currently undergoing a massive starburst. Analysis of the cluster's structure indicates that glgC-1 has a complex core, composed of two distinct sub-clusters, each moving at different speeds relative to the other. This is further supported by the detection of a large cold front in the cluster's center, signifying the movement of gas sub-clusters. The presence of a cool core, however, is disrupted by the presence of a gas tail. Additionally, the cluster's X-ray luminosity shows variability over time, suggesting that glgC-1 is currently experiencing a pre-merger phase. The data suggest that the cluster's center is composed of two distinct sub-clusters, each having a mass roughly equal to half the total mass of the cluster. This discovery provides new insights into the structure of massive galaxy clusters and their coexistence with distant, highly magnified galaxies. The observations also reveal that the cluster's center is experiencing a major transformation, likely the result of a pre-merger phase that will eventually give rise to a massive elliptical galaxy. The data collected by the JWST offer unprecedented insights into the structure of massive galaxy clusters, revealing previously unseen details of their core. The study of glgC-1 is an important milestone in the understanding of massive galaxy clusters, facilitated by the power of JWST to collect precise data on these complex celestial bodies. The discovery is the result of a collaborative effort between three scientists, who would like to acknowledge the support of the following institutions: NASA, STScI, and University of California, Irvine. The research is an ongoing project, with plans to continue the study using data from the proposed LUKE telescope, a project expected to launch in the late 2020s. This study examines a profit-sharing model between content and internet service providers, with agreements that reward sharing of costs associated with internet traffic and content delivery. Under these agreements, all parties incur fixed costs, with variable costs tied to content transmission over the internet. As a result, each ISP strives to minimize their excess costs by limiting bandwidth allocated to specific content, with content providers seeking to maximize their reach through negotiations with ISPs. Our analysis reveals that profit-sharing agreements result in reduced bandwidth allocation for content, compared to scenarios where agreements are nonexistent, with these agreements simultaneously increasing the scope of content availability and allowing providers to split costs associated with internet traffic. To further explore the effects of these agreements, we conducted a numerical study, which demonstrated their unequal impact on content and ISP profits, with agreements primarily benefiting providers in cases where their costs are low and vice versa. Moreover, we discovered that these agreements have a more substantial impact on bandwidth allocation and content availability than they do on cost splitting. Ultimately, we established that these agreements can serve as a viable means of addressing network congestion, while also facilitating greater content accessibility and potentially more equitable cost distribution among content and internet service providers. To better understand the practical implications of these findings, we developed a pair of numerical case studies that showcase the consequences of network congestion and highlight the potential benefits of profit-sharing agreements in reducing bandwidth allocation and increasing content availability. Furthermore, we investigated how these agreements interact with mergers among internet service providers, which can exacerbate network congestion and decrease bandwidth allocation, even in the absence of a global congestion crisis. By exploring the effects of these agreements on various provider structures, from duopolies to full consolidation, we identified distinct patterns in bandwidth allocation and content availability and highlighted opportunities for content and internet service providers to negotiate more favorable terms through profit-sharing agreements in consolidated markets.
