In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents a challenge, making it harder to forecast compared to individual variables. Recent research has introduced the MultiFormer model for LSTF, which incorporates transformer blocks and utilizes cross attention mechanisms specifically designed for multivariate sequences. By exploiting inter-variable relationships, MultiFormer outperforms individual predictor models in forecasting multivariate time series. This study delves into the internal dynamics of MultiFormer, examining the performance of its individual components and proposed mechanisms through extensive experiments. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of MultiFormer in tackling real-world LSTF tasks. Compared to existing baselines, MultiFormer exhibits superior results in multivariate forecasting, highlighting its potential as a robust and generalizable model for long sequence time-series forecasting. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to varying dispersion, which depends on factors like temperature, air pressure, and horizontal wind speed. To correct for this dispersion, Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors are employed, relying on precise measurements of the refractive index of the atmosphere. Current methods using micrometers and the Abbie refractometer are now supplemented with new techniques such as interferometry and ray tracing for better accuracy. Under clear skies, we measured the dispersion for six different telescope pointers at the Yunnan Observatory using these novel methods, finding significant discrepancies between the results and previous predictions. These new measurements are expected to contribute to refining the ADC system and facilitating precise astronomical observations. Furthermore, these measurements could also be utilized for investigating the properties of horizontal wind in the atmosphere. To achieve this, we plan to analyze the data from the Yunnan Observatory's systems in the future, and if necessary, establish in-situ wind measurement devices. Additionally, these new methods can serve as alternative solutions for telescopes lacking other ADC systems to operate efficiently. In the long run, these measurements are anticipated to contribute to the advancement of wind and atmospheric turbulence research. In this context, we measured the dispersion for a 2.4-meter telescope at an airmass of 1.72, yielding a value of 0.415 arcseconds. In contrast, the average value from previous predictions is 0.281 arcseconds. It is noteworthy that the difference between these values ranges from 47% to 81%, emphasizing the necessity of these new measurements for refining the ADC system. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework, which iteratively combines multi-teacher logits guided by label information, to produce a distillable ensemble. PILE has been successfully applied to several real-world ranking tasks across multiple industries, demonstrating improved performance when compared to single-model baselines. Notably, our method has shown a 5% lift in click-through rate (CTR) on a real-world search engine dataset. The source code for PILE is available at https://github.com/airbnb/rank_distill.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not possible due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. We demonstrate that, if the bosonic dark matter has a non-zero ultralight component, except for a near zero-frequency component, it can be detectable through experiments that are currently unsensitive to its direct measurement. The near zero-frequency component is a result of the bosonic dark matter's slow drift, and since its amplitude is determined by the Compton frequency, it is the most significant component for lower frequency ranges. Therefore, if this component is detected in an experiment, it implies the presence of bosonic dark matter. Experiments that are currently unsensitive to direct measurement of bosonic dark matter can be optimized to detect its presence through this near zero-frequency component, and potentially set limits on the density of bosonic dark matter. Additionally, if the bosonic dark matter is not purely ultralight but has a finite mass, it can still be detectable through this near zero-frequency component, and potentially shed light on its nature. Finally, since finite mass bosonic dark matter can be an extension of a broader class of fields, our method can be utilized to detect their presence as well. We establish that unique solutions exist in certain situations and identify the optimal choice of Kc in terms of a measure's total variation. This research also explores the recovery of Radon measures from low-frequency frequencies, including additional constraints such as bounded support within a given interval. P4 is a language used to write programs that run on programmable switches, allowing customization of how incoming packets are processed. However, validating P4 programs against the specifications of these switches, before the program is even implemented, has been a time-consuming process. We've created an automatic method to check P4 programs against the specifications, by translating P4 into a formal language, and using this translation to prove that the program is valid. This process now takes only a few seconds, and can be integrated into the development process, automatically flagging any potential issues as the program is written. We've tested this method on over 80 real-world programs, and found over a quarter of them were flagged for potential issues, many of which caused crashes when run on the switch. We've also used this method to identify and fix over a hundred potential bugs in the P4 compiler and the switch specifications, resulting in entirely error-free programs for several large programs. We've made our method available for others to use, and plan to continue improving it to further streamline the development of P4 programs. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. However, the standard finite element methods that use these elements have low spatial accuracy, specifically not more than first-order, when applied to the vector transport equation, even when higher-order methods are used for the vector field. This study presents a novel approach that uses a more robust method for transporting the vector-valued variable, resulting in higher-order approximations with a corresponding increase in computational efficiency. This methodology is particularly useful in simulations that involve complex interactions between fluids and their surroundings, such as in the study of fluid flow through a porous medium, where the assumption of incompressible flow may not always be valid. An extensive set of numerical tests demonstrates the high accuracy of this method, even in challenging scenarios, and its implementation is available online for public use. Specifically, the code can be found at https://git.xjtkj.com/xjtkj/transport_raviart_thomas by utilizing the XJTKJ library, a free and open-source library. This new approach has the potential to greatly benefit simulations involving vector transport and can be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, efficacy, efficiency, and reliability. Current discussions on deep learning often prioritize dimensions of quality (e.g. accuracy, fairness, interpretability) over those of quantity (e.g. speed, cost, scalability), even though the latter significantly influence the former. To bridge this gap, we present a comprehensive framework for the converged challenges of deep learning, starting with an in-depth examination of the interplay between different dimensions of quality and quantity. This insight enables us to analyze repeated learning tasks as a game of strategic interaction between dimensions, where dimensions of quantity can either support or impede those of quality. This framework is then applied to identify key similarities and differences among various learning tasks, which are further evaluated using a comprehensive scoring system to assess their complexity. Ultimately, our research aims to provide a unified understanding of the intricate nature of deep learning and motivate future research to address these concurrent issues. The analysis was conducted using a large dataset of 150 academic papers, consisting of 434,791 words, collected from leading computer science conferences and journals over the past 25 years. The results show promising potential for further investigation, demonstrated by an 18.4% improvement in text classification accuracy across multiple categories using a machine-learning approach over a human-driven approach. In addition, our research includes a unique visualization technique to illustrate the evolution of deep learning over the past 25 years, employing a technique called Latent Dirichletial Allocation to analyze the topics and trends within the dataset. The results show a consistent correlation between the computed quantities and those of quantity and quality, revealing a significant shift towards more effective and interpretable models towards the end of the studied period. The results are validated by means of statistical analysis and further confirmed by an expert review. The proposed framework and technique offer novel and insightful ways to understand the nature of deep learning and may be applied to other areas of study in the future. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. A crucial aspect of these methods is that they can be effectively applied to problems with significant stiffness ratios, and we demonstrate their applicability in such scenarios through several example studies. Furthermore, we introduce a method of embedding these stages in order to enhance the efficiency and compactness of the HBVM algorithm, resulting in a reduced-flops variant of the method while maintaining its energy-conserving properties. This variant is shown to be accurate and efficient in a variety of test cases, and is particularly beneficial for problems involving large systems of Hamiltonian ODEs. Additionally, we observe that this compact variant is well-suited for integration with generalized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (GHMC) algorithms, potentially facilitating more efficient use of these algorithms in various applications. Consequently, this compact variant may be a useful tool for various tasks, including constrained optimization and the integration of differential equations in robotics. The compact nature of these methods makes them particularly useful for these applications by allowing them to be more easily integrated with these tasks, as exemplified in a specific use case involving the robotics application. The compact variant is shown to be accurate and efficient in all these scenarios, as demonstrated through numerical testing. The research presented here provides a foundation for further investigations into the compact variant and its potential applications in various areas, such as constrained optimization, the integration of differential equations in robotics, and generalized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithms. The compact variant is predicted to be a valuable and efficient tool for these areas, and ongoing research is aimed at exploring its potential in these domains in greater detail. This paper introduces an innovative approach, layer group update, as a efficient way to train large neural networks. It achieves this by dividing the network into multiple training iterations, using localized critic networks to assess the effect of each group. The findings show that this method not only saves computational resources but also enhances the diversity of solutions available for large-scale neural network training. Additionally, the paper examines the potential for further improving performance by strategically selecting the layer groups to update. Using a comprehensive framework with multiple criteria, the experiment verifies that optimizing the selection of layer groups can yield improved performance compared to random updates. This study examines a three-dimensional autonomous chaotic Hamiltonian system derived from the Auer-Rasmussen-Schenck (ARS) waterwheel model, modified by Auer to account for dissipation. We observed significant changes in the system's dynamics when dissipation is minimal and non-negligible. In the absence of dissipation, the system's trajectory spans the entire phase space, whereas introducing even weak dissipation causes some regions to become escape-proof. Our findings indicate that as dissipation strengthens, these escape-proof areas shrink, ultimately disappearing at a certain threshold value. Notably, this transition occurs abruptly rather than gradually. We also discovered that areas surrounding singularities remain escape-proof throughout and that other regions exhibit complex, often unexpected patterns. Notably, some basins of attraction display break-down patterns, whereas others exhibit escape via unpredictable paths. This is distinct from Wada basins, whose borders around singularities exhibit smooth, continuous trajectories. Introducing dissipation leads to Wada basins becoming non-Wada and eventually disappearing. This is in contrast to regular basins losing escape paths but retaining their Wada characteristics. Our research indicates that small changes in a system can have significant effects on its dynamics, particularly when those changes are influenced by dissipation. This has implications for understanding complex real-world systems affected by dissipation. We also found that the concept of Wada basins applies not only to three-dimensional systems but also to systems with higher dimensions. This is illustrated in the example of a four-dimensional system, where we identified a Wada basin with escape routes surrounding a periodic orbit. Introducing dissipation in this system caused the non-Wada basins to gain escape-proof areas, ultimately resulting in the appearance of Wada basins at a certain threshold value. This highlights the importance of considering the effects of dissipation on systems, particularly when those systems exhibit complex, higher-dimensional dynamics. This is exemplified in the case of a five-dimensional system, where we identified a Wada basin with escape routes surrounding a periodic orbit and an unstable torus. Introducing dissipation in this system caused the non-Wada basins to gain escape-proof areas, ultimately resulting in the appearance of Wada basins at a certain threshold value. This has implications for understanding the behavior of systems with higher dimensions and the potential for Wada basins to exist in those systems. Our investigation into the breaking of parity and charge-parity symmetry in lepton pairs produced through the interaction of a complex spinor field with a pseudoscalar boson reveals the presence of new, long-lived states of motion in the pairs' center-of-mass frame. The pairs can remain in these states for considerable times and travel substantial distances between their point of origin and decay site before ultimately decaying. A primary characteristic of the coherent states of lepton pairs that we've identified is their ability to be stable against decay for a time directly proportional to the ratio of the square root of their total momentum to their decay constant, and their lifetime increases significantly with higher total momentum. Additionally, these coherent states exhibit no inherent momentum direction, rendering them naturally stable against decay caused by a spheron or similar long-lived particle. We've also found that, in contrast to the typical short-lived states of motion, the coherent states in question do not follow the usual pattern of decay probability gradually building up over time, but rather show an almost instantaneous buildup of decay probability as soon as the production conditions are met, and this is particularly pronounced for the coherent states with higher total momenta. It's also worth noting that, while these coherent states may not be stable against a particular type of decay caused by a spheron, they remain entirely stable against all other types of decay caused by a different type of particle. Furthermore, these findings imply that, in cases where the production conditions are met with a total momentum of at least the order of the decay constant times the mass of the spheron, the coherent states in question can be considered entirely immune to decay caused by the spheron. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capability to capture high-level temporal structures in videos through the
integration of 3D convolutional layers and attention mechanisms at two distinct
levels of the network architecture.
While the lower-level HAN captures local patterns within a video clip, the
upper-level focuses on grouping relevant clips to represent temporal sequences
in an action.
Through extensive testing on widely used action recognition datasets, HAN has
demonstrated superior performance, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a significant
margin.
Furthermore, the hierarchical structure of HAN enables the visualization of high-level
feature maps, which provides valuable insights into the internal decision-making
process of the network.
Ultimately, the efficacy of HAN has been validated through its superior results on
human action understanding tasks.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics and imply the strong form of cosmic censorship when the horizon radius exceeds a certain value. When the horizon radius is at or below this value, the weak form of cosmic censorship may be preempted, potentially allowing naked singularities to form. The underlying physical process involves scalar field scattering that extracts energy from the black hole, resulting in energy emission that influences the singularity's formation. Numerical computations of the phase shift as a function of energy for different impact parameters reveal critical points that indicate when the strong form of cosmic censorship is violated. The preconditions for these failures include when the horizon radius approaches the singular radius, or when the charge in the black hole approaches its maximum allowed value. These findings suggest that the strong form of cosmic censorship can be violated under specific conditions, but only under the influence of external scalar field scattering. The underlying mechanism involves modifying the energy-momentum tensor due to the scalar field, causing energy to be transferred from the black hole and ultimately leading to a collapse into a naked singularity. The potential for this type of phenomenon to occur is an area of future research that is both necessary and important. The mathematical framework developed for the analysis is complex and requires numerical computations to solve equations analytically. The resulting solutions indicate that the phase shift as a function of energy for different impact parameters exhibits multiple minima and maxima, indicating that the strong form of cosmic censorship can be violated under a wide range of conditions. We are investigating a simplified model of a semiconductor manufacturing system, where a continuous flow of material through a network of roads and roadsides undergoes discontinuous and stochastic changes at specific roadstops. As a result, the velocity of the material becomes discontinuous, complicating the use of traditional models in optimal control theory. To address this issue, a new approach is employed, first by transforming the material's equation into a partial differential equation with a measure solution, and then formulating an optimal control problem for the resulting equation. Utilally, we leverage the uniqueness of the solution to the adjoint equation in order to derive an optimality condition for the controlled process, and establish the ability to achieve optimal control in this context. Interestingly, an illustrative example demonstrates that even with a limited number of control adjustments, it is often possible to obtain optimal results. This model possesses a form of anti-bifurcation behavior, meaning that small changes in control can frequently produce large and irregular outcomes; consequently, obtaining accurate solutions may require the use of fine spatial meshing. To verify the model's accuracy, several tests are conducted, including comparisons between approximate and exact solutions on different mesh sizes, as well as evaluations of their convergence towards each other. These studies confirm that increasing mesh quality leads to more precise results, and that further refinement is often required to achieve acceptable outcomes. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights into the nature of the model, and could be extended to address related problems in the future. One promising direction for further investigation is the development of a multi-period version of the model, where decisions made at different times can affect the material's trajectory, and potentially interact with each other in complex ways. Another potential area of exploration is the creation of a multi-objective variant of the model, where multiple, conflicting goals must be taken into account when determining the material's path. As both of these extensions present formidable technical challenges, they are currently the subject of ongoing research and analysis. Conversely, a simpler variant of the model, where adjustments are made continuously rather than in discrete increments, has been successfully optimized and is presented as supplementary material. This continuous model is notable for producing solutions that are both continuous and regular, and is likely to be of interest to researchers working in the field of optimal control theory. Furthermore, it is worth noting that both the continuous and discrete models share a common origin, and are both guided by a set of assumptions that are presented in the accompanying document. This document also provides a detailed explanation of how the discrete model is derived from the continuous variant

For a finitely generated group G acting on a graph X, we define a growth gap as a measure of how rapidly group actions of G on X increase in size. Given a finite subgroup H of G, the first growth gap, denoted delta_1, measures the speedup in actions compared to H's actions on its own graph when applied to G's actions on X. In our study, we find a lower bound for the first growth gap in actions by a torsion-free group G acting on a tree, showing that this bound can be achieved under specific conditions. Notably, this lower bound delta_1 implies a second growth gap, denoted delta_2, is at least 1/2. We illustrate the significance of our findings through examples and explore the relationship between growth gaps and group properties such as freedom from torsion and infinite cohomological dimension. In particular, we demonstrate that a group G has infinite cohomological dimension if its growth gap is infinite, as defined by a separate criterion. Additionally, we show that a group G is non-elementary (neither cyclic nor finite) if its growth gap is greater than 1, as proven by another set of criteria. Animals move through their environments for different purposes like foraging for food, mating, or escaping predators, yet their locomotion is frequently hindered by obstacles in their surroundings. Researchers have studied how animals navigate around obstacles in free space, but there's a lack of knowledge about how they move through complex environments with multiple obstacles. To address this, we analyzed a cockroach navigating through a space with various shapes and sizes of obstacles and found that its movement can be explained using a simple and effective strategy called the elastic slider model. This model reveals how the soft-bodied nature of the cockroach interacts with hard obstacles, resulting in a predictable pattern of movement. By applying this model, we were able to accurately predict the trajectories of the cockroach and also tested its applicability to other soft-bodied animals. Our study provides new insights into the locomotion of soft-bodied animals moving through complex environments with hard obstacles. Moreover, it can be adapted for use in robotics, specifically designing robots that are inspired by soft-bodied animals. This could potentially lead to the creation of more resilient and agile robots in the future. By combining theoretical models with the actual behavior of animals, we can develop better technologies that draw from nature. Ultimately, our goal is to understand how animals move and use this information to improve robotics, while also gaining a deeper insight into the animals themselves. To achieve this, we need to simplify complex phenomena into manageable concepts, which in turn, can help us identify the key factors that determine animal movement. By doing this, we can make significant contributions to both the fields of biology and engineering. As an example, we successfully applied the elastic slider model to predict the movement of a geodesic sphere on a two-dimensional map. This demonstrates that this model can be used in scenarios beyond the testing of soft-bodied animals, and it may also be applicable to other creatures that move through complex environments. To further explore this, we investigated how the hardness of the sphere affects its movement and found that this factor has a significant impact on the predicted trajectories. This study shows that the elastic slider model can accurately predict the behavior of hard-bodied animals as well, such as a sphere that is much harder than the cockroach. This model can potentially be used in various applications, such as designing robotic spheres that navigate through complex environments, and it may also be adaptable for use in other shapes of robots, such as robotic planes or boats. Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our research, we addressed the challenge of achieving efficient surplus management by establishing a detailed model for networks with multiple-bus systems.
The study focused on extending the concepts of bus admission control, resource allocation, and surplus optimization to complex networks with multiple buses.
A two-stage approach was employed, consisting of a bus admission control stage and a resource allocation stage.
For the admission control, we developed a nonlinear programming model to optimize network benefits by selectively activating buses in the network.
Subsequently, we utilized the admission outcomes in a detailed model to determine optimal resource allocation for each bus.
A distributed algorithm was designed to achieve bus admission control and resource allocation, and the results were compared with the central approach.
The findings revealed that the distributed approach was more adaptable but yielded slightly larger gaps in optimal performance compared to the central method.
To address this discrepancy, we introduced performance guarantees for the distributed algorithm, demonstrating its efficiency and reliability despite potential performance discrepancies with the central approach.
The effectiveness of our distributed approach was also validated through numerical simulations, which demonstrated its superior real-time capabilities and reasonable accuracy compared to the central method. Ultimately, the distributed approach was found to be a more practical solution for complex power transmission networks. Further research is needed to improve the efficiency of the distributed algorithm. In this study, the dynamic structure factor and sound wave components of several borate glasses are calculated and compared with inelastic neutron scattering data, revealing a systematic discrepancy between the experimental and theoretical boson peaks of these glasses. The main objective of this study is to determine the origin and implications of this observed boson peak anomaly. Additionally, the sound wave component of the dynamic structure factor is used to extract the mechanical properties of the glasses, such as their shear stiffness, ADP-like behavior, and longitudinal and transverse sound velocities. This study further explores the relationship between the dynamic structure factor and sound wave components of the glasses, as well as their decoupling in relation to the boson peak anomaly. Information regarding the boson peak can also be obtained from vibrational density of states measurements, such as those conducted using inelastic neutron scattering or high-resolution infrared spectroscopy. As a result, the Adamantine Dynamical Picture of glasses is found to be in harmony with the principles of elasticity. Optimization methods, such as Evolutionary Algorithms, often face a challenge in achieving diverse solutions, as their primary focus is on finding the best result. Multi-Objective Optimization has addressed this issue in the past, but its solutions tend to accumulate near the optimal front, lacking variety. On the other hand, Quality Diversity search aims to produce a wide range of satisfactory solutions, but its reliance on a predefined satisfaction function limits its applicability. Our research introduces a new approach that combines the benefits of both Multi-Objective Optimization and Quality Diversity, eliminating the need for a satisfaction function and an objective function. This method, inspired by interactive multi-criteria decision-making, allows users to provide preferences for each diversity of solution. By taking into account the preferences and skipping unsatisfactory solutions, our approach guides the optimization process towards a more efficient search. Our experiments demonstrate better performance in diverse solution discovery when users provide preferences, compared to the standard optimization method. Furthermore, our approach enables the discovery of a vast number of diverse solutions with varying preferences, making it suitable for situations with complex and constantly changing environments. Our source code is available at https://github.com/alexbolc/prefqd. Our approach is also integrated into a web platform at https://prefqdiversity.github.io. Our study reveals that in the stable versions of these problems, a matching pattern can always be found where it coincides with a person's first preference for the time slots they have allocated. If the stable matchings also consider the order of their second preferences, a compatible pattern can always be found where it aligns with those preferences as well. Our research examines how static strain influences the valley Hall effect in 2D materials. By applying a continuous, smooth strain profile to these materials, we find that valley pseudospin becomes frozen and directionally directed, even though lattice atoms move. A specific, linear strain-dependent valley Hall conductance develops, separate and distinct from dynamic valley Hall effects. By comparing with existing studies on dynamic valley Hall effects, we establish a complete classification of all possible valley Hall effects in 2D materials, categorized by their origin. Moreover, we propose a new method to control valley circulation in these materials through strain, offering promising possibilities for improved performance in strained 2D electronic devices. Lastly, our study also includes a numerical analysis of valley Hall effect in bilayer graphene, showing that valley Hall effect can be completely disabled by certain strain patterns. These findings provide valuable insights for the design and operation of valley-based 2D electronic devices.

We investigate the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by the Gromov--Hausdorff distance. In this distance, two spaces are closer to each other the more their distances between points converge. By analyzing the class, or 'cloud', of all metric spaces, we identify a sub-cloud consisting of spaces that bisect along a given line, and show that this sub-cloud is well-defined and closed. Furthermore, we establish a method for approximating any metric space with a finite-adiameter 'cloud' that accurately reproduces its distances up to a specified error margin. These findings are based on a split operation that divides spaces along given lines, and a fusion operation that combines spaces along specified lines, both of which preserve distances up to a specified error margin. By combining these operations, we are able to precisely calculate the distances in the Gromov--Hausdorff distance between any pair of metric spaces, and thus effectively classify the boundaries of metric spaces, or when their distances become arbitrarily large. As an application, we show that the boundaries of all finite metric spaces are countable under the Gromov--Hausdorff distance. Featuring a simple and planar structure with microstrip feeding, the antenna is ideal for use in compact array configurations. By optimizing the size and position of the slot on the radiating patch, a substantial size reduction of over 60% was achieved with minimal impact on its radiation pattern. Manufactured from a low-cost RO3003 substrate with 1.52 mm thickness, the prototype antenna has excellent agreement between its measured and simulated performance. The outcome of this research provides a solid foundation for the development of highly compact and planar array antennas operating at mm-waves. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study creates a hybrid approach combining a Bayesian analysis and a neural network to tackle the problem of surface code decoding with measurement errors. This novel framework differs from previous methods by using a Bayesian filter to refine beliefs about the code state over time, as opposed to relying on a Bayesian estimator. Furthermore, by leveraging a neural network to map the current belief into a prediction of the code syndrome, this code demonstrates improved performance and flexibility when dealing with various error patterns, including those that cannot be accurately simulated randomly. Experimentally, this code verifies a significant reduction in decoding failure rate when compared to a leading alternative method, achieving a 45% improvement on a surface code with 32 qubits. This advancement indicates the potential for increased fault-tolerant quantum computing performance using this hybrid approach. This work is also available as a arXiv paper at arXiv:2101.02151.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter does not significantly influence the correlations and that hadrons with higher momentum fractions (approximately 0.15 or greater) exhibit suppressed yields in Au$+$Au collisions compared to $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This suppression is most pronounced for hadrons with the highest momentum fractions and is evident for various hadron types, including electrons from positron pairs. The observed pattern is consistent with energy loss experienced by partons traversing the Au nucleus, and the hadron's rapidity distribution and transverse momentum dependence of the suppression effect are accounted for by factors including final state interactions and the characteristics of the parton momentum spectrum produced in the nucleus. While the findings suggest that the parton momentum spectrum is biased towards lower momentum values in Au$+$Au collisions, a detailed determination of this bias requires further analysis. These results provide crucial constraints for the development of microscopic nuclear physics models. In digital-analog quantum computing, a hybrid approach is employed where some parts of a quantum system are treated digitally and others analogously. This study investigates the digital-analog simulation of the Hubbard model, a fundamental quantum system that describes interactions between electrons in solids. We have found that digital-analog simulation of the Hubbard model requires an optimal connectivity arrangement between qubits, with a distance of no more than two hops between any two qubits. Furthermore, for a two-dimensional Hubbard model, a fully analog simulation becomes necessary as the electron interactions exceed the allowed digital connectivity limit. We have explored a possible correction method through analog techniques and have estimated that around ten analog connections per qubit could ensure a successful simulation. Moreover, for smaller systems, a general digital-analog simulation of the Hubbard model is feasible with a qubit connectivity that doubles as a suitable number of orbitals per site. These findings provide crucial insights for implementing digital-analog quantum simulators for simulating quantum chemistry and material science applications. With this knowledge, researchers can design and build efficient digital-analog simulators for a wide range of problems, such as simulating spinless fermions with limited connectivity, fermionic systems with smaller systems, and even interacting fermions with a limited number of connections. Furthermore, for a fully analog simulation, the required connectivity becomes a fully connected graph. We have found that a fully analog simulation of the Hubbard model is feasible with a fully connected graph, while a fully analog simulation of the fermian Hubbard model is feasible with a fully connected graph for larger systems, the latter being in the near-term quantum simulator limit. A well-known phenomenon in deep learning is the 'rich representational' effect, where networks initialized with more expressive features tend to perform better, both in terms of optimization and generalization. The exact mechanisms behind this effect, however, are still not fully understood. Our research reveals that increased expressiveness in initialized representations leads to better performance by triggering the early activation of specific neurons during optimization, ultimately influencing the selection of effective sub-networks. This discovery allows us to design novel initialization methods that exploit the 'rich representational' effect, resulting in improved performance and wider applicability. Our results cover a range of network architectures, tasks, and data sets, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments. Notably, our method enables the development of compact sub-networks with up to 99% reduced size, while maintaining or even surpassing the original performance. Achieving the formation of a persistent, diffraction-limit-focused spot in highly turbulent environments is a significant challenge addressed by photonic topological insulators. However, creating a control system for an adaptive optical camera that operates in turbulent, airless environments is complex, particularly when controlling for the diverse diabatic effects that arise from interactions between light and exotic materials. Our research introduces a novel, data-driven approach that utilizes deep learning to navigate complex control dynamics and accurately predict required wavefront adjustments for both locating and maintaining a stable focus in a "dark" or black topological insulator. Through simulations, we successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in focusing a 632 nm laser beam under extreme turbulence, even when subjected to random, violent air disturbances equivalent to conditions 10^11 times greater than standard atmospheric interference, resulting in a stable focus with minimal divergence. This breakthrough method may enable the development of durable, self-sustaining optical cameras capable of operating in the most extreme environments. Furthermore, the principles of this approach could be applied to controlling light interactions in other exotic materials for potential applications in imaging and communication systems. It frames the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes as a Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, supplemented by a positive constant, and models this difference with a mean-reverting process that incorporates a lower bound. Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings indicate that, depending on the parameters of the active neutrinos, DUNE might be able to establish a limit on the mixing parameter for a sterile neutrino with a mass of approximately 0.3 GeV. The constraints we derive could be compared to those obtained from previous experiments such as TRIDENT and other contributions, as well as future ones like STOLI and BESIII, as well as potential results from the SHiP experiment. Additionally, we explore the possibility of detecting a sterile neutrino signal in DUNE with a mass less than 0.1 GeV, but this depends on various factors including the number of protons in the DUNE target. Based on our research, we recommend increasing the number of data collected by DUNE to 10 kiloton·year to enhance its sensitivity to sterile neutrinos with a mass of 0.1 GeV. Finally, we outline a suggested strategy for future sterile neutrino searches at DUNE, emphasizing the significance of accurately reconstructing event relationships and increasing the number of data collected.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials with varying sample sizes in each study often utilize cluster-robust variance estimators to account for heteroscedastic error. However, these estimators may face issues with bias and inflated type-I error rates, particularly when the number of included studies is low. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of five cluster-robust variance estimators in meta-regressions and likelihood-based models, and derive new estimators to address these limitations. Through simulations, we find that these new estimators demonstrate improved performance in terms of bias and power compared to the existing estimators. Notably, our results suggest that the new estimators are particularly effective when the number of included studies is small ( fewer than ten) and when there is significant heteroscedasticity. We also derive analytical formulas for the bias of four existing estimators, which may aid in developing corrections in the future. Finally, we apply the proposed estimators to analyze the efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines using real-world data from eight studies. The associated code can be accessed on our GitHub repository. https://github.com/mbjosey/ClusterRobustMetaAnalysis. The corresponding paper is available on arXiv at arXiv:2202.02691. \end{itemize}}

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the relationships between subtopics. Most current approaches in the field of natural language processing focus on categorizing text into predefined classes, whereas human organizers often create subcategories dynamically to group relevant information together. In an effort to address these limitations, we propose a new semantic hierarchy construction approach that allows for the creation of tailored categories with meaningful subcategories, all while maintaining a hierarchical structure that reflects the connections between topics. This approach utilizes a combination of unsupervised topic modeling and human-curated thesauri to categorize information and determine the level of co-occurrence-based subcategory refinement. Our experiments on a range of topics, including technology, finance, and sports, demonstrate that our system not only matches the performance of state-of-the-art hierarchical topic models in terms of overall topic accuracy but also excels in subcategory precision, the metric used to evaluate the quality of subcategories. Additionally, an in-depth analysis of our approach highlights both its strengths and weaknesses, and suggests potential future improvements. We examined the dynamics of non-hierarchical three-body systems consisting of a central body and two escapers at varying energies, starting from parabolic cases down to bound ones. The primary objective was to identify a universal relationship between the escape probability and energy for all scenarios, yet our results revealed distinct behaviors influenced by several factors: mass ratio, initial conditions, and whether the central body was massive enough to affect escapes. These findings imply that an accurate prediction of an object escaping a larger system, such as a star cluster, is not feasible based on simple, generally applicable formulas. The story of Halley's comet, commonly interpreted as evidence for the great comet of 1577's repeated visits due to a stable orbit, is thus inaccurately supported. Moreover, our research contradicts the notion of a "halo" surrounding a galaxy's central region, comprising objects thought to be in long-term, stable orbits. The actual dynamics in these regions is likely more complex and less understood. The wide applicability of our results to various systems, including those within our galaxy and less stable ones, is discussed. The research presented here serves as a foundation for future explorations of three-body systems, potentially shedding light on celestial phenomena. The suppression patterns of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were investigated in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy. The study was based on a dataset with 1.1 nb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, collected by the LHC. The study compared the meson yields to those measured in proton-proton collisions, considering various factors including transcription factors and scaling variables. The findings reveal that both J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons are suppressed and exhibit similar suppression patterns, but with greater suppression than those observed in previous smaller-nuclear collision experiments. Additionally, the study found that the meson suppression is not solely dependent on the initial energy density, but also influenced by the transit time of the mesons through the hot medium. The study rules out a simple scaling hypothesis that attributes meson suppression solely to initial energy conditions or transit times. A combined transit time and energy condition transit-time model best explains the observed suppression patterns. Such a model indicates an initial transit time of approximately 6-7 GeV$^{-1}$ and an energy condition that increases from 1.2 to 2.2 GeV$^{-1}$, transitioning from lower to higher centrality levels. The study also found that the ratio of prompt to total J/$\psi$, measured in the most central collisions (0-5\%), is consistent with theoretical predictions based on the model that best explains the suppression patterns. Furthermore, the study found that the average transverse momentum dependence of the suppression factor is generally in line with model predictions, but with some discrepancies, particularly for higher transverse momentum ranges above 8 GeV/$c$. Finally, the study found that the measured average suppression factor and ratio of prompt to total J/$\psi$ are consistent with those obtained from the measurement of the nuclear modification factor in high-energy Au-Au collisions at a 200 GeV collision energy, collected by the PHENIX experiment. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between the transit time of the mesons and initial energy conditions that influence the suppression patterns of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons in high-energy nuclear collisions. The findings also set the stage for future studies in smaller systems, such as p-Pb collisions, and for potential applications in the study of quark-gluon plasma properties through direct photon measurements. When software modifications are validated using a regression testing suite, 
the primary goal is to confirm that no adverse impacts have been introduced. 
However, the actual outcome may be that issues are detected beyond those 
originally present, indicating that new faults have been incorporated. 
Given this scenario, determining the optimal subset of the software modification 
history to re-examine becomes a pressing concern. 
A novel approach, using fault propagation concepts, has been developed to identify 
the most relevant changes that require re-testing. 
This method involves constructing a network where each software modification 
state represents a node, and two nodes are connected if one leads to the other 
in the testing sequence. 
Additionally, the approach employs both traditional and predictive measures to 
determine the connectivity strength between nodes. 
Results from a real-world case study at IBM demonstrate that this approach can 
identify modifications with a higher risk of containing new faults and thus need 
re-testing, and also pinpoint specific changes that testing on them could block 
the propagation of faults to subsequent testing steps. 
This method has been automated and made available through a tool called FPTNet, 
which allows users to replicate the study using their own historical testing data. 
You can access the tool at https://fptnet.github.io. 
In addition, the project has also established a fault propagation testing corpus 
comprising 81 empirical fault propagation cases derived from actual testing data 
of 7 real-world software systems, which can be downloaded from 
https://fptnet.github.io/corpora.html. 
This corpus provides a valuable resource for researchers to validate their fault 
propagation models against real-world scenarios, and also supports cross-tool 
validation and comparison experiments.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, separating them into 'S' and 'U' types based on their bar features. Our analysis revealed that U-type galaxies are generally blue, have high star formation rates, and contain old stellar populations, unlike S-type galaxies. Both S and U types, however, have similar gas consumption rates. U-type galaxies tend to have more compact bulges and are often surrounded by a dusty ring, which may indicate a recent bar formation episode triggered by a major galaxy collision. Our findings suggest that U-type and S-type galaxies share a continuous evolutionary connection. Both types are involved in active bar formation, although S-type galaxies tend to experience this process at an earlier stage, whereas S-type galaxies are more likely to have experienced a major collision and subsequent bar formation later in their lives. Our research implies a two-phase bar formation scenario, with U-type and S-type galaxies representing these stages respectively. Both S and U types continue to evolve through various processes, including internal and external interactions, resulting in diverse galaxy morphologies. Ultimately, both types contribute to the complex galaxy population observed today. In this study, a detailed analysis of the time-reversal symmetry in a model system is performed using real-time imaging of the current correlations in a network of quantum wires connected in a cubical arrangement. Our findings demonstrate that the disappearance of non-local phase shifts and Hall voltage following the introduction of a magnetic field through time-reversal symmetry breaking accurately reflects the 3D topological nature of the insulator, thus offering a 3D equivalent of the 2D Fraunhofer interferometry test commonly used to identify topological insulators in lower-dimensional systems. Furthermore, our results reveal that the time required to break symmetry across the entire sample volume grows with the linear size of the crystal and decreases with the magnetic field strength. A theoretical model has also been developed to describe the interferometry measurements, which takes into account the delay in symmetry breaking due to increased spin-orbit interactions on the surface of larger samples. Notably, our research reveals that large surface electron populations can result in significant delays in symmetry breaking, which could be misinterpreted as evidence of time-reversal symmetry in the bulk of the insulator. Consequently, a longer duration of measurement is recommended to ensure accurate results for larger samples. Ultimately, our study provides conclusive proof of the 3D topological nature of Bi$_{1-x}$M$_{x}$Te$_3$-M = Mn, Cr with a minimal concentration of 0.25% by using the non-local phase shift test. This CHO emerges when a system with time-delay is subjected to a small-scale perturbation. Notably, we discovered that periodic modulation of the time lag can amplify chaotic behavior. Furthermore, we found that systems with time-delaying mechanisms that are unrelated to each other can produce synchronized chaotic patterns. Using our technique of hidden chaotic oscillation, we were able to identify a novel type of synchronization, which we term second-order hidden chaotic oscillation (2HCO). As another application of our technique, we were able to explore and analyze a system with time-delaying mechanisms that are oppositely related, resulting in a synchronized chaotic pattern, referred to as double-hidden chaotic oscillation (DHCO). This DHCO arises when two systems, with delay mechanisms that oppose each other, are synchronized in a chaotic pattern. Lastly, we applied our technique to a delay-based model of the stock market, which revealed a hidden chaotic oscillation in the interaction between two companies. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, our findings are expanded to cover stochastic higher-order functional programs within a type-safe, affine, and higher-ranking functors framework, encompassing additional features like stochastic type abstraction. To tackle the increased complexity, our reasoning method is based on a hybrid approach that integrates denotational and operational reasoning. As a significant contribution, this study is the first to define and prove an adequacy theorem for stochastic higher-order functional programs with arbitrary rank-stochastic types within a type-safe, affine context. The associated proof is significantly more complex than previous operational adequacy theorems for higher-order probabilistic programs, requiring novel strategies for reasoning about high-order code with arbitrary probability distributions. To facilitate the understanding of our technical developments, an accompanying technical report is available, detailing our operational semantics through a straightforward presentation. Additionally, an interactive visual proof of the adequacy theorem has been created to aid with the comprehension of our formal results. Both resources can be found on our project website at https://stlc-for-free.github.io/stlc2/. As a related effort, a new interactive proof assistant, called CoSTLC, has been developed to reason about stochastic lambda calculus within Coq. CoSTLC can be used to formally prove and derive operational and denotational properties, including an adequacy theorem for stochastic lambda calculus by adapting existing techniques from stlc-for-free to reason about high-level probabilistic code. Due to space constraints, a more detailed explanation of our findings, along with the associated CoSTLC proof, can be found in a separate technical report at https://stlc-for-free.github.io/stlc2/. The source code for both projects can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/stlc-for-free/stlc2 and https://github.com/stlc-for-free/CoSTLC, respectively. The authors would like to thank Bruno Benticelli, Eugenio G. Omodeo, and other members of the project for their valuable contributions. Imitation learning seeks to eliminate the complexity and subjectivity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  However, designing feasible imitation tasks is challenging, particularly for tasks requiring multiple decision-making steps, as expert actions in these tasks are a combination of their initial states.  As a result, imitation learning often struggles to leverage the diverse range of states seen during training.  To overcome this limitation, our approach utilizes both state-dependent and task-dependent factors to create a discriminative imitation task.  By training an encoder to extract key state characteristics and a classifier to replicate expert behavior in these states, our method demonstrates improved performance, especially when dealing with tasks requiring multiple decision-making steps and a large volume of state data.  As evidence, our approach outperforms traditional discriminative imitation learning methods in a simulated driving task and achieves comparable results to behavior cloning on a real-world driving dataset.  Additionally, our method exhibits a beneficial connection to reward learning, allowing it to transfer learned state characteristics and achieve better performance more efficiently.  As a result, our method is able to achieve a higher success rate in a lane-keeping task using the TORCS driving simulator after only 10 minutes of training, compared to 1 hour required by behavior cloning.  Our method is also more sample-efficient than behavior cloning in a real-world driving dataset, achieving a 6.7% higher success rate in a lane-keeping task.  As further evidence of its efficiency, our method is also able to achieve a 14.4% higher success rate in a lane-keeping task using a large volume of state data and multiple decision-making steps without any supervision. A major uncertainty in the theoretical framework for the initial conditions of the universe concerns the amplification of magnetic fields. Our research explores how this amplification affects the formation of the first protostars through the dynamo process in the collapsing clouds of gas. By utilizing a simplified model of dynamical protostar formation, we analyzed the effect of magnetic field amplification on protostar development, focusing on its impact on the inner disk dynamics and secondary protostar formation. The results show that moderate amplification of the magnetic field by a few thousand times leads to an inner disk that can support a stable, rotating jet-forming magnetosphere similar to that observed in typical low-mass protostars. However, extremely strong amplification can disrupt this magnetosphere and give rise to an inner disk that may fragment to form additional protostars, particularly if amplification occurs early in the collapse or if amplification is localized. This implies that the fragmentation of clouds with intensely amplified magnetic fields may significantly impact the formation of the first protostars, with far-reaching implications for the formation of bound objects. Our findings also shed light on the possible amplification required to explain the observed strong magnetic fields in some primordial molecular clouds. Our research suggests that the magnetic field in such clouds must be intense enough to affect protostar formation, potentially leading to fragmentation and the formation of multiple protostars. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 2006 and 2015 examined the impact of mental health treatment as a condition of probation.  By comparing offenders who received mental health treatment with those who didn't, we tracked the offenders' within-system outcomes, like new charges and convictions, and found that those who received mental health treatment were 25% less likely to return to the justice system.  An economic model revealed that providing mental health treatment could save North Carolina's justice and social systems a significant amount of money each year.  This study shows that, in some cases, investing in mental health treatment as a part of a sentence can lower recidivism rates and save money for these systems.  This research supports and extends previous findings by identifying specific justice outcomes that are improved by mental health treatment and estimating the related financial benefits.  Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that a decision theory framework can effectively evaluate non-standard probation sentences like those that involve mental health treatment.  This research can inform policy decisions about such sentences in other jurisdictions, which are becoming more prevalent and relevant all the time.  An important implication of this research is that the connection between probation-related outcomes and financial effects can motivate justice officials to provide more effective probation-related services, like mental health treatment, in the future.  This research also has broader applications in the fields of criminology, law, and social sciences because it addresses questions about the justice system's handling of defendants who appear in court.  An additional benefit of this research is that the data sets used to analyze the connection between probation-related outcomes and financial effects can be applied to other areas within the social sciences that deal with connected systems, like the interplay between the justice and social systems, by revealing patterns in data and relationships between different systems, like the justice and social systems.  This research specifically uses transfer learning to discover connections between the justice and social systems, like the connection between probation-related charges and social services related to those charges.  An advantage of using this research is that the justice and social systems are two of the most prominent systems that interact with each other in the United States, making this a significant and relevant area of focus.  An interesting outcome of this research is that the justice system plays a significant role in determining what services the two systems provide, which is an important finding in its own right, in addition to the primary findings that probation-related outcomes are improved by mental health treatment and that these improvements are associated with financial benefits

Skin tone can be leveraged as a valuable attribute due to the skin's irrevocability and the varying skin tones of individuals. The study utilizes skin tone analysis through fundamental color tones and their combinations to create a reliable, albeit straightforward, verification system. The evaluation of this trimodal system is conducted on datasets from diverse origins, including the Holyoke Skin Tone Dataset and police body-camera footage, to assess its efficacy and compare it with voice and vision-based verification systems. The results indicate that the trimodal system outperforms its single-modal and two-modal counterparts in person verification. Furthermore, the study examines and discusses the ethical implications of using skin tone as a biometric attribute. Generating new training data through augmentation is often used to enhance existing datasets, but its effectiveness with advanced pre-trained models like Transformers and Conformer, particularly when applied to a limited dataset, is largely unexplored. This study examines the impact of training these models, including a Conformer, with augmented data and investigates the potential benefits and drawbacks. Augmenting a substantial dataset with a limited number of examples proves to be ineffective, but the approach has a positive impact when the base dataset is relatively small. However, in cases where the base dataset is sufficiently large, the additional computations may impede the model's performance due to potential overfitting. Therefore, the decision to utilize augmented data should be based on the size and quality of the base dataset. Notably, the benefits of augmented data are more pronounced for the Conformer model, suggesting that the gain in performance comes at a cost of increased computational requirements. As a result, using simpler models like Conformer, which demands less computation per training example, is recommended when utilizing augmented data. This study also compares the performance of various pre-trained models on a dataset for speech classification tasks and examines their responsiveness to data augmentation. Furthermore, the study delves into the relationship between the number of training examples and the effectiveness of data augmentation. Additionally, the study explores the potential of selecting augmented examples based on their similarity to in-domain data to improve model performance on classification tasks. Overall, the study provides insights into using data augmentation in conjunction with pre-trained Transformer and Conformer models. Based on these findings, the study proposes several best practices for utilizing data augmentation in model training. As an example, the study demonstrates how data augmentation can be used to improve model performance on various applications such as zero-resource speech translation and emotion classification. Achieving dependable data privacy while allowing data sharing can be challenging, which is why new concepts like One-Sided Differential Privacy have been developed. Based on an influential idea from Dwork et al., One-Sided Differential Privacy utilizes a public random variable to safeguard privacy, by utilizing data and this random variable to create an independent output that maintains privacy. In this research, we examine the computational overhead of One-Sided Differential Privacy by analyzing its time and space complexities. By applying a mathematical framework that analyzes how privacy-preserving mechanisms impact computational resources, we show that the time and space complexities of One-Sided Differential Privacy mechanisms can be precisely defined. This allows us to compare the efficiency of different approaches, such as those based on linear and logarithmic operations, and even independent components, like hash functions and bounded-counting procedures. This framework also allows us to study fundamental questions, such as determining the minimum computational requirements to support a certain level of privacy and efficiency. Using this framework, we conduct an in-depth study of the logarithmic mechanism, which is one of the most efficient under a specific privacy definition. By analyzing its properties, like uniqueness of output and independence, as well as its connection to sorting and searching, we show that these properties come at a cost of reduced efficiency in certain aspects. Additionally, we explore alternative mechanisms that use bounded-counting procedures with unique outputs, which, however, come with a higher computational price and fewer benefits. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the trade-offs between computational resources and data privacy, which can guide the selection of appropriate approaches based on specific requirements. As a result, our work can be applied in various contexts, such as real-time applications, data processing, and learning algorithms, which have different privacy and efficiency needs. For instance, data processing may be able to tolerate longer computational time but needs precise results, whereas real-time applications can accept rough estimates with quick computations. On the other hand, learning algorithms typically need rapid computations with minimal computational overhead. In any case, our precise complexity analysis can help determine the feasibility and efficiency of using Data Privacy approaches. Recent observations at sub-millimeter wavelengths have identified gas substructures within protoplanetary disks, a phenomenon that requires explanation. Our study presents a simulation method to replicate and analyze these substructures by incorporating a novel model into the ASTROBEAR framework. This model uses a zero-level approach to model turbulence, assuming its effects are already present in the disk's density and viscosity. Through this method, we have identified two possible origins for the observed gas substructures: either they result from the disk's own internal dynamics or from the influence of a planet. Our results demonstrate that both scenarios can produce substructures with characteristics matching those observed, although a planet's gravitational potential appears to more accurately explain the substructures' shapes and locations. To confirm these findings, we suggest that future observations account for both scenarios, incorporating signs of planet migration to explain the rapid evolution of these substructures. Our simulation model and analysis present a potential explanation for the observed gas substructures, and we invite further discussion and modification to refine our approach. Additionally, our study's results are available for reproduction through the ASTROBEAR website.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to its immense speed and volume. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these conditions, paths with specific regularity exist. In doing so, we draw on Lions-Papanicolaou-Rascorn and Tan's previous work on joint measures, while also establishing that these paths satisfy specific requirements, ultimately allowing us to extend the outcome to a broader class of mean field games involving higher-order controls. The study's conclusions are further exemplified through the analysis of a mean field game of controls for Schrödinger equations. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is one of the galactic examples that defies expectations. It possesses a rare combination of low surface brightness and robust star-forming activity, particularly evident in a prominent off-axis star-forming region. To understand the origin of this unusual feature, we conducted a photometric analysis using data from Gaia EDR3, Spitzer, and Herschel, and found that the off-axis star-forming region is likely a ring-like structure. Additionally, our findings reveal a faint, diffuse light that envelops the galaxy and extends towards the surrounding intergalactic medium, and we identified a small, companion galaxy associated with UGC 8839 through Gaia EDR3's photometry data. This newly discovered companion, which we've designated as SGS, is likely involved in the galactic merger that created the remarkable off-axis star-forming region in UGC 8839. We introduce a novel approach to quantify the influence of each training example on a classifier's performance. Notably, we find that our method can highlight problematic training samples that are also detected as out-of-distribution examples by module-based methods, indicating a strong potential for collaboration between explanation techniques to improve model robustness and reliability. This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. The specific space of matrices differs in each field: it's the integer 2x2 matrices in combinatorics, particular symmetric matrices in algebraic statistics, the Jacobian matrices of smooth curves in enumerative algebraic geometry, and a mix of both with certain constraints in topology. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. The anomalous Hall effect is found to be significantly affected by pressure due to changes in its Curie temperature and the ratio of spin Hall to s-d hybridization length. The modifications induced by pressure lead to the emergence of the anomalous Hall effect at lower temperatures and ultimately result in nearly quantized anomalous Hall resistivity at its lowest working temperature. The theoretical model based on the Landau-Büttiker formula predicts that the anomalous Hall conductivity can reach 99.99% when the temperature and pressure are optimized. The findings of our study demonstrate the potential for controlling the anomalous Hall effect through external pressure, offering a promising pathway for the design of more efficient magnetic amplifiers, spin-transfer torques in stable skyrmion textures, and other innovative technologies. The research also highlights the significance of exploring pressure-driven materials for the development of anomalous Hall materials with exceptional performance. The experimental data presented in this study were collected using a diamond anvil cell at the HPCAT beamline of the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, IUCR, and the Stanford PULSAR beamline, XSD, with a combined high-pressure and high-temperature setup. The data were further analyzed at the High Pressure Synchrotron Station, CSP, utilizing a high-pressure and high-temperature facility. Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition. Among various natural language processing (NLP)
techniques, relation extraction (RE) has emerged as a crucial method for acquiring
formal knowledge from free-text sources. By identifying specific relationships between
named entities in text, RE contributes significantly to formal knowledge acquisition.
Although substantial progress has been made in NLP, current state-of-the-art RE models
are inherently human-dependent, relying on large amounts of labeled data and
pretrained transformer language models. To break away from these limitations, we
investigate the potential of using semantic graphs as a substitute for labeled data
in RE tasks. By training a graph-based RE model, we demonstrate that high-quality
semantic graphs can serve as effective substitutes for labeled data in RE tasks. On
three standard benchmark datasets, our results reveal that the graph-based model
achieves performance on a par with state-of-the-art human-dependent approaches. When
evaluated on a more challenging dataset, our approach surpasses existing benchmarks.
Moreover, we showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to a knowledge-
graph completion task, thereby highlighting the broader applicability of our findings
to formal knowledge acquisition methods. To facilitate future research, we make our
