A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness, allowing for classification of subsets with a significantly lower measure of complexity, specifically those with complexity $O(\log^2 n)$. This improvement is demonstrated through two key findings: first, that Borel Wadge classes form a complete system for classification, offering unambiguous assignment of subsets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$, and second, that no subset with a complexity of $O(\log n)$ is classified as null or complementable. Additionally, the system's universality in categorizing Borel sets with a complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$ has been confirmed through an application of Turing's universal computation principle. This classification system has far-reaching applications in various fields, including computability theory and descriptive set theory, as evident in numerous notable results and generalizations. Notably, the classification system's utility in categorizing subsets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$ is unrelated to projective classification, as initially hypothesized, and also fails in the context of classification of $\Pi^1_1$ subsets, as exemplified by the non-isomorphic nature of classification systems with respect to Borel Wadge classes and projective classification. Furthermore, the non-uniqueness of classification of Borel sets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$ has been proven, and the non-uniqueness of classification of Borel sets with a complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$ has been reduced to a simpler form, as well as the non-uniqueness of classification of Borel sets with a complexity of $O(\log^3 n)$. Also, the classification system's inability to categorize subsets with a complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$ uniformly over all finite stages has been confirmed, and the non-uniqueness classification of Borel sets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$ uniformly over all finite stages has been proven. Finally, the unique role of Borel Wadge classes in categorizing subsets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$ uniformly over all finite stages has been confirmed. This research provides novel insights into the field of descriptive set theory, specifically with respect to the categorization of subsets with a complexity of $O(\log n)$. Similarly, the research offers fresh perspectives on the categorization of subsets with a complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging as a result of the relentless drive for higher accuracy. However, such networks pose significant challenges for computation and can be difficult to optimize via standard backpropagation during training. A novel approach, ClickTrain, leverages a combination of parallel, specialized accelerators to efficiently process forward passes and corresponding "unrolls" of differentiable operators, enabling simultaneous training of both models and their unrolled approximations. ClickTrain facilitates the joint optimization of both the accuracy and the degree of unrolling by automatically turning off unnecessary layers during training, thus enabling a more effective and timely convergence of models. Experimental results on popular computer vision benchmarks demonstrate the capability of ClickTrain to achieve superior performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing the training time by two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, ClickTrain exhibits a 2x improvement in inference latency compared to standard CNNs, representing a significant acceleration. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/UMD-WASPC/ClickTrain. In addition, a hardware-specific implementation can be found at https://github.com/UMD-WASPC/ClickAcc. Both repositories are open for public use.

This research examines the properties of a specific type of lattice, namely bounded distributive residuated lattices, and determines how their ordered groups' properties relate to their distributive residuated lattice structure. A crucial aspect of this study involves obtaining a precise description of the distributive residuated lattice components in a bounded distributive residuated lattice by applying the concept of a canonical extension. Additionally, this text explores equivalent conditions for distributive residuated sublattices within bounded distributive residuated lattices, and showcases an example of such a sublattice for a specific lattice. Furthermore, this study investigates the distributive residuated lattice homomorphisms and computes the first-order distributive residuated lattice logic algebra based on a bounded distributive residuated lattice. Finally, related results for multiplicative and intuitionistic distributive residuated lattice logics are also examined. Overall, the findings of this study provide a significant contribution to the field of distributive residuated lattice logic algebras. As a result, this study has the potential to motivate future research on higher-order distributive residuated lattice logic algebras based on non-commutative bistructures. A fundamental aspect of exoplanetary science revolves around understanding how a host star's properties influence the characteristics of its associated planets. Previous research identified a correlation between a star's metallicity and the presence of giant planets, prompting further investigation into the properties of smaller, sub-Neptune and Earth-sized planets. Contrary to expectations, no clear relationship between a star's metallicity and the presence or size of these planets was found. To address potential biases in this study, the characteristics of the sample stars were examined in relation to their metallicities. The analysis revealed that older, metal-rich stars are more likely to be selected for planet size studies due to their lower luminosity and the limitations of current detection methods. Additionally, it was found that these selected sample stars tend to have higher radial velocity dispersion and gas consumption rates, indicating that older, metal-rich stars are more likely to have lost planetary systems. These findings suggest that the age and metallicity of a host star should be taken into consideration when interpreting the size distribution of exoplanets, and that existing detection biases may be responsible for the lack of observed relationships between a star's properties and its associated planets. To further understand the planetary population, the authors advocate for incorporating age information into future planet size studies, particularly for smaller, cooler planets, where current detection methods are influenced by a star's properties. The authors also suggest exploring alternative detection methods, such as transit photometry, which are less dependent on a star's properties, to gather age and metallicity information for a larger sample of host stars. By combining these approaches, researchers may be able to obtain a more accurate representation of the planetary size distribution and its relationship to its host star properties. This research presents an innovative method for accurately segmenting handwritten mathematical symbols in mixed-script equations. The approach utilizes a novel pixel-based segmentation algorithm that leverages the principles of sequential Monte Carlo methods. To achieve this, we introduce specific features tailored to detect mathematical symbol junctions, and apply a range of geometric shape filters to handle diverse symbols. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through its performance on the MathQA dataset, revealing high segmentation accuracy rates of 67% for handwritten equations and 92% for machine-printed ones. Furthermore, we achieved a significant reduction in processing time to less than 200 milliseconds, making it suitable for application in real-time mathematical equation recognition and analysis tasks. The proposed method shows great potential in addressing the complex challenge of handwritten mathematical symbol segmentation. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical application in high-dimensional robotic systems is often hindered by slow exploration resulting from the high dimensionality of the action space. To address this challenge, actor-critic methods can be integrated with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a global optimization technique that has been successfully applied in various machine learning tasks. In this research, three HMC variants for use with actor-critic reinforcement learning are presented, each of which leverages either the Hamiltonian, its gradient, or a hybrid metric for sampling. To evaluate their effectiveness, these variants are integrated with PPO and sampled in both a direct and indirect manner in simulation environments based on simple robots. The results indicate that the integration of PPO with HMC results in improved performance, particularly when sampling indirectly. The most effective variant involves using the hybrid metric for sampling. The success of this technique is attributed to its ability to leverage the Hamiltonian and its gradient, which is particularly beneficial in high-dimensional action spaces. To verify its real-world applicability, this research is conducted using a 7-DoF robotic arm in a reach-and-grasp task, and the results show that the integrated system achieves high success rates in this task. It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. This characterization allows us to define a set of possible values for $k$ that result in prime numbers $p$. This set, denoted as $\mathcal{K}$, can be precisely defined by two elements: the set of numbers greater than $\frac{p+1}{6}$ and the set of numbers greater than $\frac{p-1}{6}$. Furthermore, the difference between the largest and smallest elements of $\mathcal{K}$, represented as $\delta(p)$, measures the size of the set $\mathcal{K}$. By calculating $\delta(p)$ for various values of $p$, we derived the maximum value of $\delta(p)$ for $p$ in the range of $5$ to $37$ million. Additionally, we identified the lower bound of the difference between the twelfth smallest and smallest elements of $\mathcal{K}$, denoted as $\tau_{12}(p)$, and $\tau_{11}(p)$, and the upper limit of the difference between the twelfth smallest and smallest elements of $\mathcal{K}$ for $p$ in the range of $5$ to $37$ million. This comprehensive study provides a substantial advancement in the knowledge of $\delta(p)$, $\tau_{12}(p)$, and $\tau_{11}(p)$. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic technique that enables the computation of $\delta(p)$, $\tau_{12}(p)$, and $\tau_{11}(p)$ for all $p$ up to $393$ million with an efficiency of $13.59$ hours, utilizing $40$ processor cores. This computational speed is significantly faster than the previously reported $1.52$ hours on $128$ cores. This advancement enables the storing of $\delta(p)$, $\tau_{12}(p)$, and $\tau_{11}(p)$ in a database, thereby providing instant access to these values. This database can be used to verify numerous instances of maximum $\delta(p)$, $\tau_{12}(p)$, and $\tau_{11}(p)$ values that were previously unverified. Nereid, a moon of Neptune that has not been visited by a spacecraft in over 25 years, exhibits an enigmatic spectrum. Its complex appearance can be broken down into two distinct components: a featureless blue visual color and a reddish hue in infrared light. Multiple theories attempt to explain the spectral variation, including the presence of icy particles, carbon and silicate dust, and even tholins, all contributing to a better understanding of this unusual object. To further analyze Nereid's colors, we employed a new approach, utilizing principal component analysis (PCA) to identify linear combinations of synthetic spectra that accurately reproduce the observed colors. By applying PCA to Nereid's synthetic spectra, produced through the MIE model, we identified two distinct components that can explain the spectral variation. The first component is associated with particle size, while the second is linked to complex organic molecules. Our findings support the application of PCA to analyze spectral data, as it can help to both linearize complex spectral patterns and reveal features difficult to detect through traditional analysis. Additionally, this approach can facilitate the comparison of synthetic and observed spectra. Based on this comparison, we found that the PCA-derived colors align closely with the observed colors of Nereid. As a testament to its effectiveness, this analysis was applied to two other TNOs, Kala and Ukko, whose spectra also showed a similar variation, as observed in Nereid. Overall, our study demonstrates that PCA can be a valuable tool in spectral analysis, especially when combined with the MIE model and other computational methods. This approach can be expanded to other complex spectral data and can potentially reveal new insights into the composition of celestial bodies. Ultimately, this research may contribute to a better understanding of the spectral variation in neutral-sloped TNOs and other objects with similar color patterns. In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within these models. This analysis provides insight into the relationship between cardinal characteristics of the continuum and the existence of these reals in specific models of set theory. As a consequence, it can be concluded that certain model properties are equivalent to each other, particularly in the context of random and Cohen reals. This result is also extended to other related concepts, such as S-space and null- and split-rational sets, yielding novel characterizations of these concepts within specific models of set theory. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that certain model properties can influence each other's values within these models through a process called'model inheritance.' Ultimately, this analysis enables the precise determination of the values of specific cardinal characteristics in specific models of set theory, such as $\mathfrak{d}$, $\mathfrak{s}$, and $\mathfrak{q}$, and provides a positive answer to a question initially posed by Brendle and Shelah in 2002 regarding the relationship between additivity number of null- and split-rational sets, thereby establishing a novel application of set theoretic techniques to model theory. This research has further implications in the context of selection principles in set theory, particularly in relation to the long known but unpublished result of Magidor that $\mathfrak{s}<\mathfrak{q}$ in $L(\mathbb{R})$, which can now be attributed to Pawlikowski's earlier work. This analysis ultimately culminates in a comprehensive survey of recent findings on the topic of set theoretic geometry within models of set theory. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in suboptimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this issue by limiting actions with little or no data coverage. Although most pessimism-based methods rely on a universal Q-function or a universal policy, these assumptions are unrealistic and lead to suboptimal results. Our approach addresses these limitations by assuming only access to an offline oracle providing the expected reward under any given action and state. A pessimism-based value function is defined, related to the actual value function through a regret bound, and a pessimism-based policy is developed, achieving a connected relationship with the optimal Q-function and a related regret bound. The proposed method is shown to be effective even when the coverage condition isn't met and requires no additional assumptions. Our approach is implemented in a variety of contextual bandit scenarios, and both theoretical and experimental results demonstrate its efficacy. For instance, in the contextual bandit scenario with multiple actions, our approach achieves a $1-\gamma$ guarantee for the first-action advantage, meaning that our method's performance is within $1-\gamma$ of the optimal Q-function value compared to the first action's value function. The approach is evaluated in various scenarios, including a dialysis treatment study, with results showing its effectiveness and efficiency in creating a dynamic treatment regime when given offline data and no universal policy or Q-function assumptions. The method is available at https://github.com/alexeydud/bayes_pessimism. The dialysis treatment study is based on data from a 2018 University of Pennsylvania IRB-approved study. The method's performance is evaluated using data from the study, as well as other public datasets, including dialysis treatment data and COVID-19 contact tracing information. The approach is shown to effectively create a dynamic treatment regime for the dialysis treatment study with partial coverage, and its efficiency in creating a pessimism-based policy without universal assumptions is demonstrated through a comparison of running times for various methods. The efficiency of the method is further evaluated in a COVID-19 contact tracing study with limited data coverage. The results of both studies indicate that our approach is effective and efficient in creating a dynamic treatment regime for the dialysis treatment study with partial coverage and is capable of running on a personal computer. The method is shown to be ineffective in creating a dynamic treatment regime for the COVID-19 contact tracing study with limited data coverage.

We have expanded Miyashita's duality's implications for tilting modules over Artin algebras, and in the process, we have derived new expressions for the endomorphism space of the dualizing module in terms of a tilting module's adjoin and restriction functors. Our findings align with earlier work by Iyama and Ree, and can be seen as a particular instance of their more comprehensive results. Building on this, we have formulated a duality theory for Morita dual pairs of finite type abelian categories with a dualizing module. This has led us to a generalized version of Miyashita's duality for such categories, which shares similarities with a duality theory proposed by Goto and Iyama for categories with a strong duality. Additionally, we have identified a tilting module for which the endomorphism space of the dualizing module is a hereditary artin algebra, and as a consequence, we have derived new expressions for the endomorphism space of the dualizing module in terms of the tilting module's restriction and kernel functors. Our results also enable the computation of the endomorphism space of the dualizing module for certain tilting modules of type A and D. Furthermore, we have established a connection between our duality and that of Zhang for Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as a generalization of her findings for tilting modules. Finally, we have applied our duality to calculate the endomorphism space of the dualizing module for certain tilting modules of type A, B, C, and D. The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. We also examine the validity of this theorem for other types of topological groups. Additionally, we establish the uniqueness of the a-adic solenoid among topological groups that satisfy this functional equation with specific functional properties. This leads to identifying the solenoid as compactly generated and having a countable basis. Furthermore, we show that the character group of the solenoid has a similar structure and apply this to determine the solenoid's rational representation. We also identify a new class of topological abelian groups connected to a-adic solenoids and provide examples that illustrate the groups' distinct topological properties. Finally, we consider a non-abelian generalization of the Polya theorem for linear combinations and power functions, identify the solenoids that satisfy this relationship, and establish their topological properties. We also establish a non-abelian version of the Polya theorem for solenoids based on global fields, including their finite extensions and field extensions of prime degree. We conclude by highlighting the solenoids' distinct topological properties and investigating their connection to topologically simple groups. Partially, our results align with existing findings from other researchers, while some findings presented here introduce novel ideas. We present our findings in a way that is approachable for those familiar with local fields and topological groups, along with providing necessary background information on the character groups of topological groups, functional equations, and solenoids based on global fields. Presence-absence data is frequently incomplete due to detection limitations in ecological studies. This deficiency is likely to be unbalanced, with more records of one species than others in a particular site. Our research explores two approaches for handling such imbalanced data: standardization and rarefaction. These methods are often used for comparative analysis of species diversity across different sites, but we demonstrate that they can also be applied to compare species presence across various environments. We examine the impact of these methods on the resulting data and find that while they make data more comparable, they also introduce bias, particularly the tendency to overrepresent more common species. To address this issue, we propose an alternative method based on the entropy of species presence-absence data. This new method aims to provide unbiased species presence data by evenly distributing the presence probability of each species across different environments. Our results indicate that the proposed entropy-based method not only produces more balanced species presence data but also preserves more information about species presence-absence patterns compared to the standard methods. Furthermore, this method allows species presence data to vary across different environments more realistically. Ultimately, the choice of method depends on the research objectives, with the standard methods being more suitable for species diversity analysis and the new method being more effective for species presence prediction. Our study provides a framework for handling imbalanced species presence data, and the associated R code is available upon request. Additionally, a package named BalData is under development to automate the process. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has achieved significant progress. Directly predicting the saliency map from the input image is difficult, thus many methods utilize auxiliary information to facilitate extraction and prediction. In this paper, we propose an innovative method that employs a cross-attention context extraction module to integrate the global context with each pixel's local features. By doing so, our model accurately identifies the salient region and effectively bypasses manual segmentation, making it more efficient. Furthermore, our method is designed to be versatile and can be combined with various backbone networks for improved performance. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model, and it is available on our GitHub repository for public access. Our model is also formulated as a unified framework for contrastive learning, enabling self-supervised pre-training before fine-tuning with labeled data. This two-stage training approach significantly improves the accuracy of the model. Thorough ablation studies are also conducted to evaluate the proposed method's performance. Our proposed method achieved state-of-the-art performance on the SalientObjectDetection dataset, outperforming other methods by a substantial margin. Additionally, our self-supervised pre-training approach shows promising results, laying the groundwork for future research in unsupervised salient object detection. Computed Tomography (CT) is a widely used imaging technique that produces high-resolution, three-dimensional data with fine detail. Yet, traditional CT scans employ polyenergetic X-ray sources, which introduce two main imaging artefacts: beam hardening and photofluorescence. To overcome these limitations, the utilization of monochromatic X-ray sources becomes essential. Interestingly, it has been discovered that, in certain cases, the photofluorescence effect can be positively harnessed to enhance image contrast, a phenomenon known as 'fluorescence enhancement'. To investigate this phenomenon in detail, a mathematical framework and software tool are proposed for accurately measuring the 'fluorescence enhancement' ratio under real-world conditions. This proposed tool will be particularly beneficial in the optimization of optical and X-ray energy pairs for medical imaging applications. To validate its effectiveness, the proposed 'fluorescence enhancement' ratio was measured using realistic X-ray and optical propagation simulations in a phantom, which were both experimentally verified and found to be accurate. This study demonstrates that the proposed 'fluorescence enhancement' ratio can be calculated reliably using CT numbers and optical transmission values, which in turn can be obtained through CT scans and optical projection imaging, respectively. To facilitate the calculations, a dedicated software program, called FluE, has been developed and made publicly available for other researchers and practitioners to utilize. Finally, the potential of utilizing the 'fluorescence enhancement' phenomenon not only to mitigate beam hardening artefacts but also to minimize their impact through optimization is explored. This could be achieved by selecting an optimal optical and X-ray energy pair to counteract beam hardening effects while maximising 'fluorescence enhancement' for improved contrast. This research has significant implications for the development of enhanced medical imaging technologies. To this end, various energy pairs are evaluated and their potential in contributing to either beam hardening or 'fluorescence enhancement' is assessed. This study culminates in the recommendation of a specific energy pair for its suitability in 'fluorescence enhancement' and minimal beam hardening artefacts. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data. This problem is particularly prevalent in accessing and deciphering ancient documents from various parts of the world, rendering their text undecipherable. This study tackles the issue of low resource HTR by adopting a novel approach that utilizes only an input image and a limited dictionary of known words to produce a valid transcription. This dictionary-based HTR model is inspired by connectionist temporal classification (CTC), allowing the network to explore possible spellings of the input by concatenating and separating handwritten words. To effectively utilize word-based prior knowledge, the model segments the handwritten text into individual words based on pre-defined dictionary entries, thereby ensuring accurate representation of these word units in the feature space. Furthermore, the model incorporates a confidence mask to mask out less confident regions of the handwritten text, preventing the introduction of significant noise during the optimization process. Experimental results on the NUS-WHT-9 dataset reveal that this proposed model achieves a word accuracy rate of 0.694 @ 0.95, surpassing the performance of the baseline ctc-based approach with a word-based prior (WBP-CTC) with a word accuracy rate of 0.681 @ 0.95. Additionally, ablation studies on the NUS-WHT-9 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing word-based prior knowledge and confidence masking in enhancing the accuracy of the proposed model. To further evaluate the proposed model, a comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art approaches on the IAM dataset was conducted, revealing that this proposed model achieves a word accuracy rate of 0.876 @ 0.95, marking a notable 4.4% improvement over the baseline ctc-based approach with a word-based prior (WBP-CTC) with a word accuracy rate of 0.832 @ 0.95. In addition, the proposed model was found to have 2.3M parameters, indicating its parameter efficiency in comparison to the baseline ctc-based approach with a word-based prior (WBP-CTC) which had 13.3M parameters. To facilitate reproducibility, the proposed model's code has been made publicly available on the repository https://github.com/zhengyuyang1997/LR_HTR. We have developed a novel storage approach for low-energy continuum eigenfunctions, allowing us to compute three-body bound and continuum states effectively. A three-dimensional array is used to store the continuum eigenfunctions, resulting in a straightforward retrieval process. This method, coupled with the Euler-Maclaurin prescription, facilitates the calculation of three-body continuum-bound transition amplitudes and, by extension, decay widths. This approach can be combined with the Kowalski-Hugies method to determine continuum-bound amplitudes, leading to a rapid summation of decay widths for numerous continuum-bound states. We applied this method to calculate the $E_{\lim 3max}$ truncation error and derived formulas for selecting continuum-bound states in the no-core hyper-spherical method. This approach can be adapted for more complex nuclear systems, such as four-body systems, by integrating it with existing reactivity tools. We have demonstrated its efficacy in computing three-body decay widths with low $E_{\lim 3max}$ values and outlined a strategy for achieving this with higher $E_{\lim 3max}$ values, including a pre-selection of continuum-bound states. Furthermore, we have calculated the $E_{\lim 3max}$ truncation error for several three-body systems, showing its dependence on the decay widths of the states below it. This method can be used as a quick estimate for the required $E_{\lim 3max}$ values, enabling the development of more efficient four-body calculations. We have presented an initial four-body calculation using this method, demonstrating its potential to reduce the computational time and memory requirements by two orders of magnitude compared to existing methods. This method can be used as a starting point for more advanced four-body calculations with even larger $E_{\lim 3max}$ values. Furthermore, we have extended its applicability to five- and six-body systems, computing three-dimensional continuum decay widths for $^{10}$B and $^{12}$C with high $E_{\lim 3max}$ values. This method can be used in future calculations involving even more complex systems, such as seven- and eight-body systems, and may be particularly useful in applications involving non-relativistic quantum few-body systems with low-energy continuum eigenfunctions. Due to its versatility, this method can be adapted for use in various frameworks, such as the Klein-Harrison, Thompson, and Belyaev-Bartlett-Fowler models, and may be especially useful in reactions involving energies close to the continuum threshold. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, it identifies compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on the Bergman space of the unit ball, as well as the Bergman space of the bounded convex domain with smooth boundaries. Furthermore, this research discovers a new necessary and sufficient condition for compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on the Bergman space of the bounded convex domain, specifically where its M\"obius transformation inverse is compact on the domain's boundary, generalizing a previous finding by Zhao and Kong. Finally, this study provides compactness criteria for composition operators with bounded symbols on the Bergman space of the bounded convex domain with nonlinearity properties at its vertices, representing a significant extension of previous research by Zhu and Kong. These results significantly contribute to the understanding of compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces of various domains. Moreover, this study utilizes the second Montel theorem, the Riesz-Hilbert identity, the integral operator norm estimate, the measure theoretical lemma, the weak compactness of polynomial sets, the compactness of the composition operator on $A^2(\Omega)$ with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure), the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\Omega)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\Sigma)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\mathbb{B}_n)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\Omega)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(U)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\mathbb{D})$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\mathbb{B}_n)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\Omega)$, the compactness of the composition operator with a bounded symbol on $A^2(\Omega)$ as well as several other significant research findings.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a modified version of the positive-loop-level recursion relations in supersymmetric amplitudes, incorporating the effects of non-trivial boundary conditions at infinity. The derived amplitude is expressed through a novel set of 'zigzag' integrals that combine the 'log' and 'unlog' components from the two-loop strings of Friedman, Rastelli, and Zaffaroni. A specific transformation matrix, which relates the amplitude to these zigzag integrals, has a clear string-theory interpretation as a combination of various 'logs' and 'unlogs' present in the two-loop strings. The amplitude also contains an 'exceptional' component that arises when the external gravitons are concentrated at the boundary of the AdS space and is a non-trivial extension of the analogous component at the one-loop level. The derived amplitude is the first of its kind at the two-loop level and is specifically tailored for applications involving the collision of extended objects in the AdS space. It is expected to be useful in the calculation of amplitudes involving the collision of D3-branes in the flat spacetime and may also find applications in the study of the black-hole scattering at the NLO level in the flat spacetime. The derived amplitude is also significant as it may be used to test the feasibility of using the 'zigzag' integrals as a replacement for the more conventional 'dual-resonance' and 'logarithmic' integrals in the calculation of the two-loop amplitudes in the Minkowski spacetime. The results presented in this study may also be used to verify the level-four SUSY quantum mechanics and the SUSY coupling constants at four loops as proposed in a related work by Friedman, Rastelli, and Zaffaroni. A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also discusses the significance of Poisson's ratio in determining straw tube stability and includes an measurement of the ratio for a particular type of tube. The described method can be utilized to measure the mechanical properties of similar tubes. The intention is for this method to contribute to the development of more robust, reliable, and efficient straw tubes for future particle detectors. The measurement method can be further applied to compare the mechanical properties of different straw designs, helping optimize their performance. Our study also addresses the MARmax$^\dagger$ problem, which seeks the highest marginal probability when the optimal decision function may not exist. This model is applied to the zinc K-edge in zinc oxide, showing that at the zinc K-edge, the majority of non-linearity can be attributed to core-level excitations, whereas a pre-edge region is more sensitive to excess photons. It is also feasible to modify the model so that it can be employed in time-resolved XANES experiments where the time-dependent behavior can be isolated. As an example, the model is used in experiments on two materials: LaMnO3 and Bi4Ge3O12 doped with Eu, demonstrating its capability to differentiate between various excitation mechanisms. The model is found to be highly versatile and can be used across a wide range of materials and experiments by making adjustments to its parameters. We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. The convergence of our warping technique is guaranteed, even at the equilibrium points where warping and resolvent compositions cease to be individually contractive. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through the inclusion of examples that illustrate its effectiveness in solving complex Nash equilibrium problems with a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions in various contexts. The time complexity of this asynchronous method is shown to be comparable to that of synchronous methods based on extragradient and Newton-type iterations. A key advantage of our proposed algorithm is its ability to address a broader range of Nash equilibrium problems, including those with vector-valued action spaces and reference functions. The main contributions of our work are as follows. Firstly, we present a novel asynchronous algorithm for solving Nash equilibrium problems by decomposing mixed strategies through warping resolvents, thus addressing a broader class of problems. Secondly, we provide a concurrent framework for solving Nash equilibrium problems by leveraging warping resolvents, thereby enabling the solution of simultaneous Nash equilibrium problems even in the presence of action space dimensions. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. By leveraging the relationship between Gegenbauer polynomials and Bessel functions, we establish a convenient framework for analyzing the positive definiteness of Bessel functions, connected to Fourier transforms, and, by extension, radial functions, related to covariance operators. Our study reveals key findings on the positive definiteness of Bessel functions, $I_\alpha$ and $K_\alpha$, for specific ranges of $\alpha$. Furthermore, we establish the positive definiteness of $I_{1/2}$ and $K_{1/2}$ for any space dimension and demonstrate the positive definiteness of $I_\alpha$ and $K_\alpha$ for $\alpha \in (0, 1/2]$. The (strict) positive definiteness of radial functions is determined based on the positive definiteness of Bessel functions and the underlying space dimension. Our findings provide explicit conditions for the positive definiteness of radial functions, connected to covariance operators, and illustrate our theoretical outcomes through several examples. Moreover, we present two applications of our study: the first concerns stochastic processes, and the second relates to spectral measures in harmonic analysis. The provided stochastic process example is confirmed by simulating a 2D random process, while our harmonic analysis example is supported by numerical experiments in 1D. The associated code is available in the repository [1].

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This is analogous to classical oscillations that occur when a heavy particle moves out of the inflationary horizon. Recent research has demonstrated that either primordial features or these classical oscillations can be responsible for the generation of dark matter. This work investigates the overlap between these theoretical concepts, identifying areas of coincidence and divergence between their underlying assumptions and predictions. As a result, the study finds that this coincidence is precarious and may be lost with further advancements in certain inflationary scenarios involving a heavy field. On the other hand, models featuring a light field in inflationary models are more resilient to such disruptions, potentially holding the key to accurately describing the early universe. The study also explores potential observational signatures stemming from this overlap, including the possibility of cross-correlations between dark matter overdensities and inflationary field fluctuations. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of exploring the interface between modern inflationary and dark matter theories. Several open questions and avenues for further investigation are also presented. Specifically, the work raises concerns about the adequacy of the single-field approximation in describing the very early universe and its potential impact on our understanding of cosmic inflation. Additionally, the study ponders whether the future Dark Energy Survey will be able to detect cross-correlations with inflationary fields, thus shedding light on the early universe dynamics. Lastly, the research hints at the potential for new cosmological signals waiting to be uncovered, which could have significant implications for the understanding of cosmic structure and the future of cosmology as a field.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a quartic graph is defined as t-PH-compliant if there's a perfect matching of K_G that can be divided into t pairings, where each pairing of G corresponds to a perfect matching of K_G. We present an infinite family of t-PH-compliant quartic graphs for every value of t from 1 to 5, and also demonstrate that for any given t greater than 5, we can find a quartic graph that is t-PH-compliant but not (t+1)-PH-compliant. This achievement involves the use of high-tech graph linear control theory. By setting up a finite-dimensional linear control system with B-spline coefficients, we can determine a graph's quartic nature and perfect matchings through system trajectories. By selecting specific system parameters, we can construct quartic graphs with the desired PH-compliance properties. By contrasting these parameter selections, we can also construct t-PH-compliant graphs and their non-compliant variants. These constructions apply to any value of t up to 5, and for any value of t greater than 5, we can choose suitable quartic graphs from the infinite family. In our study, we also present computational evidence suggesting that some graphs may possess the PH-property, and we present an algorithm capable of verifying this property in certain graphs. In particular, using this algorithm, we can confirm the PH-property of all snarkian graphs with orders up to 46, and we present the results of our computations in an accompanying table. In a separate study, we found that none of these graphs have a Hamiltonian decomposition. In an effort to expand our understanding, we attempted to apply the algorithm to stronger conjectures, such as the Pairing-Hamiltonian property (PH-property) and Pairing-Matroid Hamiltonian property (PMH-property), but were unable to verify these properties for any graph with order greater than 34. We present two examples that illustrate ill-posedness and non-uniqueness of the Cauchy problem for specific differential equations. These examples demonstrate the critical role that initial conditions play in the problem, highlighting its dependence on the data and the direction of time. Furthermore, we note that these equations admit smooth, smooth-sensing solutions but with undesirable properties, such as unbounded derivatives with respect to the direction of time, thereby justifying the focus on the limited and well-behaved subset of smooth solutions. Our analysis reveals that these equations, although well-behaved within this subset, exhibit inherent flaws, making the Cauchy problem even more problematic when considering the broader class of weak solutions. Interestingly, these examples share a common characteristic of being coercive, implying that they have a unique, smooth, and continuous extension to the whole space, despite the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem. This behavior contrasts with the standard scenario, where a coercive equation typically has a well-defined, smooth Cauchy problem. Our study also explores the intermediate cases, where the Cauchy problem becomes partially defined, featuring a combination of smooth and weak solutions. Ultimately, we investigate the limiting cases, where the Cauchy problem loses all meaning, is partially defined, or remains unchanged, depending on the properties of the equation. Our findings are further generalized to a broader class of equations by analyzing their intermediate behaviors, as well as the inhomogeneous versions of these examples. In the process, we encounter new difficulties and observe intriguing differences in the behavior of the Cauchy problem for equations with and without translation invariance. In the course of our study, we establish a key criterion for the uniqueness of the Cauchy problem, thereby offering a valuable tool for the analysis of differential equations. This criterion proves particularly useful in distinguishing between well-posed and ill-posed problems, as well as in identifying equation-dependent characteristics and the importance of initial conditions. Our investigation of the Cauchy problem is comprehensive, encompassing continuous, discrete, and space-averaging versions of the problem, as well as initial value problems in the presence of noise. Our study is further enhanced by a range of supplementary findings and observations, including the behavior of the Cauchy problem for partial differential equations, differential systems with constraints, and equations on halfspaces and boundaries. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received significant attention for their ability to generate detailed images based on text input alone. However, generating high-quality images of complex subjects, such as horses, without a clear reference image, is still a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach, called Semantic Guidance for Auxiliary Images in Generative Diffusion Models (SEGA), which enables the use of text-based semantic guidance to improve the quality of images generated from auxiliary inputs. SEGA can be utilized in multiple techniques, such as providing implicit semantic constraints to existing images or supplying explicit semantic hints to image transformations. By integrating SEGA into, for example, CLASSIC, a text-to-image diffusion model, we demonstrate its effectiveness in producing high-quality, semantically accurate images from unseen references, such as equines, and also in refining existing images with precise semantic details. SEGA's flexibility allows it to be applied in a wide range of text-to-image generation tasks. You can view our generated images at https://sega-diffusion.github.io/. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have been driven by two key concepts: 1) Bayesian learning for separating prediction uncertainty from uncertainty associated with model assumptions, and 2) regularisation through maximally uncertain outputs. However, the latter concept relies on an inaccurate assumption that maximally uncertain predictions come from parameters far from the optimal solution, an idea challenged by experiments. This study introduces a new approach that analytically disentangles prediction uncertainty and assumption uncertainty in neural networks, confirming that parameter distance is not a reliable indicator of prediction uncertainty. This finding is also generalisable to other forms of regularisation. Our method is based on an analytical calculation of the predictive posterior and assumption uncertainty for a simple neural network. This calculation relies on an iterative approach to compute the posterior by alternating between optimisation and prediction. The resulting formulation reveals that assumption uncertainty is related to the eigenvalues of the Hessian and the direction of the gradient. This led to the development of a new form of regularisation based on bounding the posterior assumption uncertainty, a concept previously linked to maximally uncertain outputs. However, our results show that this form of regularisation is actually based on a dense region of the parameter space rather than its boundary. This study also shows that a common form of variance regularisation is actually an overestimate and can lead to overregularisation. Our method is more effective and can be computed analytically or approximated through sampling, outperforming existing methods such as MC-Dropout and variational autoencoders. This study is the first to provide a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of Bayesian deep learning and provides a new approach to regularisation and uncertainty quantification. The code is available online.

Analyzing the temporal characteristics of these features over eight hours, it was found that their orientations are random and uniform across the entire solar surface. Data spanning a year (2010) revealed that magnetic bright points appear at all latitudes, while their occurrence peaks between 30 degrees and 60 degrees solar latitude. Their latitudinal distribution remains relatively consistent throughout the observation period. A total of 105,460 magnetic bright points were identified during the analysis, and their areas and diameters were found to follow a normal distribution. The areas of these features range from 0.0001 to 10 square arcsec, while their diameters vary between 0.5 and 5 arcsec. The frequency of magnetic bright points peaks at 2 arcsec, corresponding to an area of approximately 2 square arcsec. The results of this study indicate that magnetic bright points are likely associated with tiny magnetic flux concentrations, and their characteristics provide a baseline for future high-resolution observations of the solar photosphere. A future high-resolution experiment called METIS on the GLXS spacecraft is expected to observe the solar photosphere at a resolution of up to 50 meters per arcsecond, providing valuable insights into the dynamics of the solar atmosphere. METIS is planned for launch in 2024.

The rapidly evolving weather system demands almost real-time weather forecasts to ensure safety. Traditional weather forecasting methods, relying on numerical weather models, often need hours to yield forecasts, yet their accuracy is limited. By leveraging the immense data from weather sensors and imagery, deep learning can facilitate quicker and more accurate forecasts. Nonetheless, direct prediction in high-dimensional weather spaces from raw data is impractical due to computational constraints and data scarcity. To address these challenges, we introduce a Video Swin-Transformer for spatiotemporal weather analysis and forecasting. By segmenting the weather space into non-overlapping tiles and processing them in a hierarchical manner, our approach circumvents the computational difficulties of direct prediction. Moreover, it extracts context-specific features from weather patterns, enhancing feature learning. During training, we utilize augmented temporal dimensions via data augmentation to incorporate variability, thus improving the model's ability to foresee future weather conditions. By evaluating our approach on real-world weather datasets, we demonstrate its superiority over existing models and showcase its potential to provide accurate weather forecasts for diverse weather phenomena, even with limited data. Finally, our approach outperforms others in forecasting the trajectory of a weather phenomenon over time. In this work, we investigate various extended scalar electroweak models characterized by $\mathrm{G} \mathrm{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{hh}$ reactions, with particular emphasis on models featuring dark matter candidates. The study focuses on four distinct scenarios: (i) an extended scalar model with $\mathrm{Z}_2$ symmetry, where the dark matter sector comprises two scalar fields; (ii) an extended scalar model without $\mathrm{Z}_2$ symmetry, where the dark matter candidate is a pseudoscalar field; (iii) an extended gauged $B-L$ model with $\mathrm{Z}_2$ symmetry, where the dark matter sector comprises three gainoes; and (iv) an extended extra gauge model without $\mathrm{Z}_2$ symmetry, where the dark matter candidate is a vector-like bino-like state. The analysis reveals that while the first scenario faces significant suppression from unitarity and collider searches, the second one can evade these constraints more effectively. Furthermore, potential signatures of dark matter are identified in the Sun's core for the remaining two scenarios, with the hadronic and semi-hadronic modes being particularly important. Additionally, the study finds that in the fourth scenario, the dark matter signal can be suppressed by a factor of roughly two by a small vector-like doublet, while in the third scenario, the dark matter signal can be suppressed by a factor of roughly two by a small $B$-$L$ doublet. The results of this work demonstrate that in these extended scalar electroweak models, the dark matter signal can be suppressed by introducing additional scalar fields that interact with the dark matter candidate. In the context of the fourth scenario, this suppression can arise from a tiny vector-like doublet that the dark matter candidate can couple to. For the third scenario, the dark matter signal can be suppressed by a small $B$-$L$ doublet. Consequently, the introduction of these additional scalar fields offers promising avenues for exploring dark matter candidates in complex scalar electroweak models. Ultimately, the dark matter signal can be potentially detected by future direct dark matter direct detection experiments such as CRESST, LUX-ZEPLIN, and XENONnT with the presence of the $\mathrm{hh}$ resonance, provided that the parameters of the model are set appropriately. Most current deep learning-based motion deblurring techniques require access to blurred data or pairs of blurred and sharp images. However, obtaining synthetic blurred data can be challenging due to the need for precise motion tracking and weight calculation, making it computationally expensive. To address this issue, we present an innovative framework that learns from sharp images only, utilizing adversarial training to induce blur simulation. This approach relies on a motion prior learned from real-world blurry-sharp image pairs, which is then applied to the model to transform sharp images into deblurred versions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing high-quality motion deblurring results from only sharp images, significantly outperforming existing methods that rely on blurred data. Additionally, we show that our motion prior can be utilized to improve existing methods by fine-tuning them with the learned blur simulation. The source code for this framework is available at https://github.com/zhengzhi-ai/learn2deblur.

Scientific breakthroughs in disciplines like astrophysics, climate modeling, and protein structure prediction often rely on computational models that are evaluated using diverse scientific data. However, the effectiveness of these models can vary significantly from one type of dataset to another. Traditional benchmarking methods typically assess models using a single dataset, or multiple datasets with a standardized format, and rank them according to their performance. Yet, other scientific datasets may exist that have not been utilized for benchmarking, or may require special processing or integration to align with the typical dataset used for benchmarking. 

In this study, we investigate a novel approach to benchmarking, in which models are applied to their respective scientific tasks while maintaining the uniqueness of each dataset. Our method employs machine learning data integration techniques to fuse traditionally analyzed data with unprocessed dataset components, such as raw data or alternative analyses. By doing so, we expand the scope of benchmarking to encompass a broader range of scientific data models. The integration of new data dimensions may lead to unexpected discoveries and significantly alter the ranking of computational models. To effectively communicate our findings, we utilize dimensionality reduction and visualization methods to compare original and transformed data landscapes. As a case study, we apply our proposed method to the field of protein binding site prediction, where traditional and new data sources are combined to identify binding sites on protein structures. The results show that the models' rankings change when evaluated using the mixed data landscape, rather than individual data components alone. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have seen significant use in handling complex, data-driven problems with intricate relationships. By integrating a series of convolution layers with traditional backpropagation frameworks, GCNNs have shown great potential in solving non-convex optimization tasks. However, the conventional use of the cross-entropy loss function, paired with the binary logarithmic likelihood ratio, can result in convolution layers that lose their differentiating capability as the network progresses, hindering the network's performance. This paper presents an alternative approach to binary cross-entropy loss, based on the cumulative gain, and evaluates its effect on the differentiability of convolution layers within GCNNs, demonstrating a substantial improvement in the classification accuracy of several benchmark datasets. Moreover, the proposed binary cross-entropy loss has been found to accelerate the convolution layer's learning process, as indicated by the increased gradient magnitude compared to the traditional approach. This results in a more efficient convolution layer, as observed in the reduced training time for the convolution layers. This study ultimately shows that the cumulative gain-based binary cross-entropy loss can enhance the classification performance and speed up the training of convolution layers within GCNNs. Experiments have been conducted on six binary classification datasets, comprising both small and large scale datasets, to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results indicate that the cumulative gain-based binary cross-entropy loss outperforms the traditional approach in 5 out of 6 datasets, with a notable improvement of 4.44% average accuracy and a reduced training time of 1.94 times. Notably, the proposed approach has been found to have a negligible computational overhead compared to the traditional approach. Based on these findings, it is recommended to use the cumulative gain-based binary cross-entropy loss as an effective alternative to the traditional approach in binary classification tasks. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven to be a significant challenge, particularly when working with new languages or domains that have limited resources available. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel, iterative annotation technique, starting with an initial, partially annotated dataset. This technique utilizes the model's predicted dependencies to guide human annotators during the labeling process, effectively making use of suboptimal predictions on the current dataset to inform annotations on the next one. Our experiments on six languages have shown that this approach consistently leads to substantial gains in parsing accuracy, with an average improvement of 6.6 F-score points, and can even surpass the results achieved by models trained on fully annotated datasets. Furthermore, we have discovered that our technique has a positive correlation with the distance between the current and target annotation distributions, and has identified two key factors contributing to its effectiveness: the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and its capacity to transfer knowledge across domains. Based on these findings, we believe that our iterative annotation method will be a valuable tool for enhancing neural dependency parsing on partially annotated datasets. We investigate first-order logic's capacity to count specific configurations within structured data sets, particularly graphs, to determine if a concept is explicitly defined. Our analysis reveals that the ability to count these configurations, or CFI-queries, is not inherently subsumed by conservative extension properties in graph classes, as evidenced by multiple counterexamples. However, we find a more subtle relationship where the consistency of certain predicate logic systems over these graph classes is necessary and sufficient for CFI-queries to be expressible within those systems. Building on this, we establish a set of necessary and sufficient conditions, tied to the consistency of predicate logic systems, for the existence of CFI-queries in these classes. These conditions are particularly important for finite graph classes, as they imply the absence of CFI-queries in such classes when inconsistent, as well as the presence of CFI-queries in such classes when consistent, under a certain condition. Furthermore, this result does not generalize to broader classes of first-order definable graphs. Additionally, we find that the ability to count 1-configurations, or CFI-queries, is not inherently subsumed by another type of logic, $\forall\exists$-definable graph classes, as evidenced by a separate set of counterexamples. However, we find two separate classes of graph configurations where both types of logic are capable of expressing CFI-queries, as well as another type of logic, locally finite, which is also capable of expressing CFI-queries in these classes. Finally, we find that a type of logic, guarded, is not inherently subsumed by locally finite, as well as another type of logic, negation closed, which is also capable of expressing CFI-queries in these classes. Interestingly, negation closed is found to be the only one of these four types of logics capable of expressing CFI-queries in these classes, as well as another type of logic, first-order, which is also capable of expressing CFI-queries in these classes. Additionally, we find that first-order is the most expressive of these five types of logics for CFI-queries. Finally, we establish that first-order is capable of expressing a broader class of first-order definable graph configurations, as well as another type of logic, locally finite, which is also capable of expressing this broader class of first-order definable graph configurations. Additionally, we find two separate classes of graph configurations where both types of logics are capable of expressing this broader class of first-order definable graph configurations

To achieve this, we create a finite sample statistical test with a specific alternative hypothesis, tailored for cyclic n-tuples. We then investigate the distribution of test statistics for large sample sizes, leading to a framework for asymptotically powerful tests in this domain. We validate our approach by deriving test statistics along with their distributions for specific instances, including polynomial functions of two variables and powers of a single variable in multiple contexts. Our analysis reveals novel test statistics, along with distributions for familiar tests like the chi-squared and Fisher's exact test, providing new insights into their performance. We illustrate our findings through various numerical examples that highlight our methodology's capabilities. Ultimately, our research contributes to a framework enabling the development of powerful tests for complex statistical hypotheses involving multiple variables and a wide range of functional forms. A related software package is available for reproduction and further exploration of our results at the following link: https://git.io/LeMxYW. We anticipate our research to have practical applications in fields where complex data often necessitates the use of high-degree functions and where the occurrence of cyclic n-tuples may indicate a significant underlying pattern. Many software systems can be customized through their run-time settings, but this configuration often results in unnecessary features remaining enabled, impacting system properties like binary size, resource usage, and performance. This unnecessary enablement can be mitigated by optimizing the configuration, a process known as run-time configuration optimization (RCCO). To date, RCCO methods primarily rely on theoretical models and controlled experiments to determine the best configuration, but these approaches are impractical for large-scale systems involving hundreds of settings and thousands of possible feature combinations. Furthermore, they do not adapt to changes in system behavior that may arise from software updates or bug fixes. To address these limitations, we present a novel approach that allows for the adaptive optimization of system configurations through machine learning by leveraging actual system measurements during run-time operation. Our approach, machine-learning-based run-time configuration adaptation (MLRCA), can identify the most suitable configurations for various system properties without relying on explicit models or quality metrics, making it more scalable and applicable to a broader range of systems, including those that cannot be modeled accurately. By retro-fitting MLRCA to four real-world systems, we demonstrated its effectiveness in producing favorable configurations, particularly in reducing feature interaction effects, resulting in performance improvements and smaller binaries. While MLRCA showed potential, it also exhibited some instability and struggled with adapting to significant system changes, highlighting the need for further improvement, especially in these areas. By addressing these challenges, we believe MLRCA can become a more reliable and practical solution for run-time configuration optimization. We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confining potential, based on an effective model that incorporates the particle's active force and a parameter representing the strength of interactions with surrounding particles. This model is used to calculate a rate function, which describes the likelihood of observing specific power inputs, and this calculation is validated through comparison with numerical simulations. The results show that both the free and confining cases exhibit similar large deviation behavior, but the rate function is more complex when an active force is present in the confining potential, particularly exhibiting local minima and maxima. Additionally, the probability distribution of power inputs is only marginally different between the free and confining scenarios for small active force strengths but diverges significantly at higher strength levels. These findings provide a framework for distinguishing between active and passive dynamics in systems governed by confining potentials, and highlight the importance of considering the interplay between these forces and external constraints. The study also underscores the value of exploring large deviation techniques in the analysis of dynamic systems. The rate function obtained in this study can be used to estimate the probability of observing specific power inputs in both free and confining scenarios, and may be applicable to the study of various biological motion, such as ciliary motility and protein transport. The effective model developed in this work could serve as a useful tool for understanding these phenomena, by facilitating the identification of active force parameters through comparison with experimental data on power input and velocity. The study further reveals that the dynamics of the active force-driven AOUP in the confining potential are controlled by a set of effective variables, which are found to be velocity, angular velocity, and the conserved momentum associated with the active force, in addition to the parameter representing interactions with surrounding particles, and the curvature of the confining potential. These findings demonstrate that the active force-driven dynamics in the confining potential are essentially three-dimensional, in stark contrast to the two-dimensional nature of free active dynamics. The study also highlights the significance of non-essential conserved quantities in the dynamics of both the free and confining active force-driven AOUP, and their impact on the generation of power input, which is found to be influenced by the parameter representing the strength of interactions with surrounding particles, and the active force strength in both scenarios, as well as the curvature of the confining potential in the active force-driven dynamics in the confining potential. The study provides new insights into the role of active force and potential curvature in dynamic systems

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across various ages and styles. Previous attempts to adapt neural models from English to other languages have required significant retraining, often necessitating multiple steps and extensive updates for each target language. We present a general framework for efficiently translating neural models from English to multiple other languages, with the option to fine-tune if desired. Our approach utilizes cross-lingual transfer, leveraging parallel datasets in both source and target languages to refine a single set of model parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in a series of systematic evaluations, achieving superior results compared to current state-of-the-art methodologies when translating neural models into multiple languages. Notably, our results show that our approach produces better outcomes when fewer target-language fine-tuning data are available, making it a more robust method in practical applications. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being a prominent frame work in this domain. It utilizes past frames to enhance present ones, but disregards spatial relationships within each frame. In our research paper, we introduce an upgraded version of BasicVSR, called UperSR, which includes two advanced features: second-order grid propagation and alignment guided by flow. The UperSR model outperforms BasicVSR and other state-of-the-art methods in various scales and frame propagation lengths, also demonstrating reduced computational complexity while achieving comparable results in many scenarios. We have developed a general approach for creating the highest-performance protocols in finite-time, stochastic heat engines, even when faced with limitations in bath temperature and scaling parameters. The overall efficiency is maximized by balancing the energy gain from the heat source and the entropy increase in the heat bath, leading to a geometric interpretation as level set of an ordinary differential equation. In the case of a given, unchanging scaling parameter, this level set can be found through an optimal control problem with a Pontryagin function that includes both a thermodynamic and a switching cost. For a constant scaling parameter and thermal bath in contact with a heat source, the maximum-efficiency protocol becomes periodic and can be expressed through a difference of two switching curves based on the past heat energy and current entropy. Additionally, we have derived analytical expressions for the maximum efficiency in both quasi-static and finite-time cycles, specifically for a harmonic oscillator and a two-level system. Furthermore, we have investigated how the maximum-efficiency protocol can be achieved in a series of discrete, constant-time steps, even when the system dynamics are not known in advance. The study includes numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applicability of these findings. Ultimately, we have established a fundamental relationship between the maximum-efficiency protocol and the system dynamics, which can be represented by a first-order differential equation. Finally, we have explored the potential for using machine learning to parameterize the maximum-efficiency protocol, even in complex systems with high-dimensional state spaces. This study provides a crucial bridge between theory and experimental practice in the field of stochastic heat engines. As such, it has the potential to inspire innovative, experimentally-verifiable designs in the field of finite-time stochastic heat engines. This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess the potential damage to power substations, the study employs a probabilistic model formulated as a linear programming problem, linked to a probabilistic map showing the likelihood of flooding in different areas. This model is applied to the 2003 hurricane season, with particular focus on Hurricane Isabel, to calculate the total cost of generating capacity losses and repair costs for all affected substations. Our results indicate that considering both hurricane and storm surge situations significantly increases the total cost of damage compared to scenarios that only account for hurricane conditions. Furthermore, the study shows that storm surge events affect a larger number of substations and causes greater economic losses than hurricane-related flooding. On average, storm surge events account for 65% of total damage, while hurricane events account for 35%. Notably, the study reveals that storm surge events impact substations that are not directly affected by hurricane winds, thus highlighting the importance of factoring storm surge into hurricane risk assessments for a more comprehensive understanding of hurricane-induced power outages. Overall, the proposed model can aid utility companies and grid operators in developing more effective hurricane mitigation and damage prevention strategies by taking into account storm surge events. Additionally, the study's findings can inform insurance policies related to power grid damage, with potential applications in cost-benefit analyses of storm surge protection measures for power grids. Based on our analysis, the study suggests that investing in storm surge protection may be beneficial if the cost of such investments is less than the expected reduction in damage costs. Specifically, our results indicate that a 10% return on investment can be achieved with storm surge protection costs amounting to 35% of the total damage, which is equivalent to $1.4 billion in our study scenario. Ultimately, the proposed model can contribute to a more accurate assessment of hurricane risks and benefits, thus enabling grid operators to make more informed decisions about investments to enhance grid resilience. We identify that the invariant sets of these maps, comprising the images of the initial domains after repeated applications, exhibit fractal properties and effectively cover the spaces in which they are defined. To mark the onset of chaotic behavior in these maps, specifically the point at which the invariant sets begin to exhibit fractal structures, we introduce a concept of a 'bifurcation map'. We calculate numerically the bifurcation maps for the generalized heterochaos baker maps in 2D and 3D spaces and analyze their behavior in relation to varying parameters. Additionally, we apply a method of 'embedding' to generate 3D fractal structures from 2D ones, and demonstrate through calculations that the topological properties of the 2D bifurcation maps can be preserved in their 3D counterparts under embedding. These findings provide a basis for exploring the potential of the generalized heterochaos baker maps as models for generating complex three-dimensional structures through layering of two-dimensional patterns.
